# The Odyssey,
## These are the most elegant and delightful twenty-four books of the oldest and most skillful Father of all Poets, Homer / concerning the ten-year wandering of the world-wise Greek Prince Ulysses / described / and now for the first time diligently translated into German by Master Simon Schaidenreißer / called <term>Minervius</term> <note>A "humanist name" adopted by the author, referring to Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom and weaving.</note> / currently town clerk of the princely city of Munich / explained with <term>arguments</term> <note>Short summaries or "plots" preceding each book.</note> and brief <term>scholia</term> <note>Interpretive notes or commentary intended to explain the text to the reader.</note> / also augmented with a biography of Homer / most pleasant to read.

->Reader, before you pass judgment, do not regret reading the preface.<-

# We, Ferdinand, by the grace of God,
->King of the Romans, forever Enlarger of the Empire,<-
->in Germany, Hungary, Bohemia, Dalmatia, Croatia, and<-
->Slavonia, etc. Infante in Spain, Archduke of Aus-<-
->tria, Duke of Burgundy, Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, and Wur-<-
->ttemberg, etc. Count of Tyrol, etc. We acknowledge that our and the Empire’s dear and faithful Sig-<-

mund Minervius, town clerk of Munich, has humbly informed us how he—for the sake of good instruction and learning, as well as for the praise, honor, and glory of all estates both high and low, and especially for the common good and the advancement of this prestigious work—has undertaken to translate all and every book of the **Odyssey** and **Iliad**, as they are called, by **Homer**, the father of all poets, which describe and recount the ten-year wandering sea voyage of King Ulysses, etc. He has transferred and brought these from Latin into the German language and intends to have these same books printed, issued, and brought to light by our and the Empire’s faithful Alexander Weissenhorn, book printer at Augsburg. However, he fears that once the said books are thus produced, they might immediately be reprinted by others, whereby his great effort, diligence, and labor, along with the investment and expenses he has applied to them, would result in disadvantageous loss and damage. And so he has called upon us and petitioned us with humble diligence that we might graciously deign to assist him in this matter with our merciful help and provision. Since it is not just that anyone should suffer harm by having their own effort, labor, and expense—especially that which is applied to such a praiseworthy, common, and good work—undermined, or that others should draw the profit from it; therefore, so that this aforementioned Minervius's practical undertaking is not abandoned or hindered due to the aforementioned concern of expected loss, we have considered his humble prayer. And for this reason, with timely counsel and certain knowledge, in the name and on behalf of the Roman Imperial Majesty, our dear Brother and Lord <note>Referring to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>, and also for ourselves, we have given and granted this <term>Privilege</term> <note>A legal protection similar to a modern copyright, granting the holder exclusive rights to publish a work for a set period.</note> to the same Sigmund Minervius. We give and grant him this also herewith by Roman Royal and Princely power, knowingly by virtue of this letter. Thus, he may have the indicated books, the **Odyssey** and **Iliad**, and whatever they are called, by **Homer**, issued in print by the named Alexander Weissenhorn as mentioned above. And for six years immediately following the date of this our letter, no one, whoever they may be, shall reprint them, nor shall such a reprint be carried about, sold, given away, or traded in any way or manner, neither in the Holy Empire nor in our other Kingdoms, principalities, and lands. And we therefore command, in the name of the said Imperial Majesty and also for ourselves, all and every subject and faithful person of the Holy Roman Empire and all our other Kingdoms, principalities, and lands, and especially all book printers, woodblock cutters, and booksellers to whom this our letter is brought and shown, or who see and read the print thereof: [We command this] Earnestly under penalty of six <term>marks of pure gold</term> <note>A significant monetary fine; a 'mark' was a unit of weight for precious metals.</note>, half of which shall fall to our and the Empire’s Treasury, and the other half to the aforementioned Simon Minervius <note>The text here switches from "Sigmund" to "Simon," likely referring to the same person, Simon Schaidenreißer.</note>, to be paid without fail. And we desire that none of them shall reprint the aforementioned books, as they are printed by the said Alexander Weissenhorn, within the prescribed time of six years, nor allow such reprints to be carried about or offered for sale, nor do so themselves in any way, as they value avoiding our and the Empire’s heavy displeasure and punishment, and in addition, avoiding the aforementioned penalty along with the loss of the reprinted books. These [reprinted books] the often-mentioned Alexander Weissenhorn may take and bring into his hands wherever he encounters them, and you shall allow him to seize them on behalf of the authorities and shall provide him with assistance in this regard. This we mean earnestly, as witnessed by this letter. Given in our Royal castle at Prague, the first day of September, in the year etc. thirty-seven <note>1537</note>, of our Roman reign the seventh, and of the others the eleventh.

->**Ferdinand**<-

# Preface.

According to the meaning of the saying by Horace <note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace’s famous principle in *Ars Poetica*: "prodesse et delectare," meaning that art should both perform a "useful" function and provide "delight."</note>, those writings are rightly considered the best and most pleasing to everyone which provide the reader with both usefulness and pleasure or entertainment. Without contradiction, the poem or writing of the most learned, ingenious, and eloquent poet, Homer, should be preferred above all others and praised, loved, and read most highly. In this work, the prince and father of all poets describes the sea-voyage of the most patient and much-traveled hero, Ulysses <note>The Latin name for Odysseus, the protagonist of the Odyssey</note>, so skillfully, orderly, and elegantly that for every person of the world—among all secular books—nothing more fruitful (in my opinion) could be found, written, read, or devised to stir the heart and love for virtue, to provide experience in many things, or to guide reason in all kinds of worldly wisdom. Nor could anything be more lovely or suitable for driving away boredom or melancholy than

<margin>Cicero, in the fifth book of his *Tusculan Disputations*.</margin> these incomparable books of Homer. In them (as Cicero testifies), all lands, regions, cities, the images of all things, wars, battles, voyages—yes, even the character, nature, and essence, not only of humans but likewise of irrational animals—are so magnificently and accurately depicted that it is truly said: The blind Homer saw all things. Furthermore, the highly wise and learned are in agreement that Homer’s writing is a praise of virtue and a clear, true mirror of human life. In it, everyone—high or low, of whatever age, gender, or status they may be—can look upon themselves and easily discern what is honorable, useful, and fitting, or what is not; what should be followed or fled; and what should be done or left undone. And especially, under the name and person of Ulysses, the most excellent portrait of a wise man is presented. He does not throw himself into obvious danger of body and life out of personal recklessness, curiosity, or boldness for the sake of loot and worldly wealth. Instead, he first seeks reasonable means and ways—even under the guise of feigned

<margin>Cicero, in the third book of *On Duties*.</margin> madness <note>Refers to the legend that Ulysses tried to avoid the Trojan War by pretending to be insane, plowing his fields with salt until his ruse was discovered</note>—to find an escape, so that he might be spared from the campaign, the looting, burning, devastation, bloodthirsty raging, and countless other evils (which follow war in heaps without measure), and instead remain in peace with his wedded wife and dear child. But since he was specifically called upon by the King of Kings, Agamemnon, in the name of the common knighthood and by the sworn duties of all of Greece, and was diligently sought and requested by peer princes and lords, he set aside not only his land and lordship of Ithaca, but also his elderly parents, his most gracious wife Penelope, and his only, still young son. Out of dutiful obedience, for the sake of honor and the common fatherland, he marched into the most dangerous war. By this, he gives everyone to understand that no one should separate themselves from the common burden, and that love and loyalty toward the fatherland and the common good—as well as obedience toward rightful authority—should be placed above all kinship and personal advantage in times of necessity...

<meta>catchword: be placed</meta>

<summary>This preface introduces Homer's Odyssey as the pinnacle of literature, balancing entertainment with moral instruction. It highlights Ulysses (Odysseus) as a model of wisdom who prioritizes duty to the state over personal desire.</summary>

be preferred. As then he, Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>, clearly demonstrated with his deeds during his long, wandering journey home after the destruction of the most powerful kingdom of Troy. For what (I ask) can happen to a person on earth from adverse fortune, which this patient and steadfast hero did not struggle against for ten whole years on land and water without ceasing, driven by his innate longing for his fatherland? First, in battle against the Ciconian people, and the man-eating Laestrygonians <note>original: "Lestrigones"</note>, and especially in the murderous cave of the inhuman, one-eyed giant Polyphemus. Secondly, on the Tyrrhenian sea and near the Malian mountains, from where Fortune struck him back nine whole days' journey, drove him into the narrows of the Sicilian sea, and threw him toward the two terrifying sea monsters Scylla and Charybdis, wherein his companions were pitifully swallowed and drowned before his eyes; he barely escaped on a plank near the island of Corcyra, cast onto the shore naked and bare; at last coming into his land and court under an unknown, despised form, mocked by the wanton suitors and even by his own household servants; all of which he bore with patience,
<margin>Cicero, *On Duties*, book 3.</margin>
and so, as Cicero writes, he waged war not only with enemies, but with the storms of the sea. And although the most victorious conquerors of nations are often overcome by bodily pleasure and their own bold, lewd, and impetuous stirrings of the mind—such as drunkenness, anger, and disorderly love—yet the Homeric hero could not be overcome or captivated by the honey-sweet food of the Lotus-eaters <note>original: "Lothophagier"</note>, nor could the sweet-singing sea monsters or phantoms, the Sirens, deceive him; nor the witch or sorceress Circe enchant him with her powerfully poisonous drink; nor could the most eloquent and beautiful goddess Calypso persuade him to forget his beloved fatherland and accept a restful, safe, and idle life with her. Also, for greater proof of his steadfast mind, he ventured into the mournful, dark region of the deceased, held conversation with the spirits, sought counsel and guidance from the seer Tiresias, and attempted, experienced, and constantly overcame all perilous things—remaining unconquered by wine, pleasure, love, wind, Fortune, sea monsters, giants, hell, spirits, and the gods themselves, by means of the most healthful herb <term>Moly</term> <note>A magical herb mentioned in the *Odyssey* that protects against sorcery; here interpreted as a symbol for wisdom.</note> (that is, wisdom), which was initially poured and planted into the noble blood and precious Ulysses from above, by the grace-giving and patron of arts, the planet or star Mercury, through the cooperation of Minerva. With this he was adorned so that he appeared so wonderful, beautiful, lovely, worthy, and pleasing before the eyes of the Phaeacians, that the royal daughter Nausicaa desired the foreign, naked, shipwrecked man as a spouse, and King Alcinous together with the Queen desired him as a son-in-law and co-regent of their kingdom. From this it is clearly understood that nothing is more beautiful or gracious than virtue, and that this is recognized by all the world, even among the Bar—
<margin>Cicero, in a letter to Dolabella.</margin>

is esteemed by barbaric <note>original: "barischen"; likely "barbarischen" (barbarian), a term used by the Greeks for all non-Greek nations</note> peoples as a thing of high worth; it is held to be—and indeed is—an eternal, immortal, and unchangeable good, much like the soul itself. <margin>Saint Basil <note>original: "Diuus Basilius"</note></margin> This virtue leaves its possessor neither in life nor in death; indeed, it swims out of the sea with the shipwrecked man and follows the prisoner even into the dungeon. And just as **Ulysses** provides an example of a worldly-wise, discreet, and much-experienced brave man, so too is the noble, beautiful, chaste, serious, and sensible **Penelope** masterfully depicted and set before our eyes as an exemplar for the female sex. She does not let her wedded husband depart from her sight and heart all at once; rather, she wakes and she sleeps with fervent thoughts and sighs for him. During his long absence, she seeks no pastime in dancing, leaping, singing, gaming, or social wandering; she remains in her ladies' chamber, sitting among her maidens. There she weaves and works with her hands all the long day and through the greater part of the night; she lies awake, pleading and mourning, so that in twenty years her bed was never dry from the tears of her eyes. One hundred and forty noble, upright, and rich youths were unable—neither through service, prayer, gifts, love, suffering, threats, nor any manner of ruinous trouble or harm—to turn the faithful, honorable, and chaste heart of **Penelope** away from **Ulysses**, who had first possessed her love and constant mind. And so that she might preserve her chaste body, her honor, and her faithfulness (truly the noblest treasure of women under the sun) for her aforementioned husband—protecting it not only from guilt, blemish, and shame, but also from all suspicion and gossip—she flees the company of men as much as possible. Whenever she must go among them out of unavoidable necessity, to answer them or to offer an admonition, she dresses simply and covers her face with a veil, so that she might not perhaps provide any enticing provocation to wicked thoughts. She also does not step forward or sit down beside them, but remains standing alone at the threshold; she speaks of her concerns with few words, and not at all with flattering or endearing speech. Furthermore, she always does this in the presence of two handmaidens, who are witnesses to her words and deeds, her actions and omissions. Quickly she returns again to her chamber to perform the business that belongs to a mother of the house. Nor does she believe lightly, nor let herself be moved by every wind; but only after certain true signs <note>A reference to the secret of their immovable wedding bed, which only the true Ulysses would know</note> that can neither deceive nor fail, she receives and recognizes **Ulysses** as her beloved husband. In like manner, the old **LAERTES** and the young **TELEMACHUS** are sketched by **Homer**, so that from their example, the fatherly heart with its natural love toward children, and in turn the duty, obedience, and respect of pious children, may manifest as clearly as the bright day. Also, if anyone seeks the office of the authorities over their subjects, or the duty of the citizenry toward their overlords, or of the servants or handmaidens toward their masters, he finds such...

<meta>This page continues the translator's preface, moving from the specific example of Penelope's virtue to a broader defense of Homer as the ultimate source of all wisdom, philosophy, and princely education. # Preface
<sig>iij</sig>

honorable and other matters which are fruitful for one to know who wishes to be in the world, described so delightfully and expertly in many places, as if it were painted out with distinct colors. And truly, among the other divine gifts with which **Homer** was richly filled, it is quite wonderful that—having flourished two thousand five hundred and twenty-six years ago—he measured and composed his writings, sayings, and maxims so skillfully that they harmonize so perfectly with every era, every age, and every custom, habit, and institution, as if no change had ever occurred in so long a time. 

I will intentionally pass over in silence the common opinions and sentences regarding the omnipotence of the **first mover** <note>original: "ersten bewegers"; a philosophical term for God or the primary cause of motion in the universe</note> of all things, of eternal providence, and of unavoidable fortune and misfortune—imposed upon everyone at the beginning of their planting <note>meaning: their creation or birth</note> by the Creator, which the philosophers call **fate** <note>original: "fatum"</note>—and also how far man's free will extends; likewise, of the nature and immortality of the soul. Regarding all of these, **Homer** speaks more formally and closer to the right path than many philosophers. 

Nor will I recount the countless brave moral sayings and teachings with which **Homer's** books are so full that it is not said unbelievably that **Homer's** writing is the true ancient philosophy and pure books of discipline <note>original: "zuchtpücher"; manuals for moral upbringing and etiquette</note>. From these, not only all poets, but indeed all philosophers—and especially the divine **Plato**—sucked their arts, and the greatest conquerors of the world were taught in honor, virtue, magnanimity, and praiseworthy government. For Master **Maximus Tyrius** and **Quintilian** aptly compared him to the great sea, indicating that just as all flowing waters and springs take their origin from the sea, so too has **Homer** given to all who follow a beginning of artistic invention and writing. 

For this reason, he is praised by <margin>Plato, *On Poetic Frenzy* <note>original: "de Poetico furore"</note></margin> **Plato** as the very best and most divine poet, a master of life; <margin>Pliny, Book 2, [Chapters] 25 and 27 <note>original: "Pli. li. 2. 25. &. 27."</note></margin> by **Pliny** as a prince and progenitor of all art and antiquity, a living, welling spring of high understanding and knowledge; and by the invincible Emperor **Justinian**, he is called a father of virtue. **King Alexander**—the greatest in name and deeds—was accustomed to calling **Homer** nothing other than a "Royal Poet," as if he meant to signify that kings, princes, and future ruling lords should primarily be instructed and raised in art, virtue, and magnanimity from the books of **Homer**, as was the custom and princely discipline in ancient times. 

<margin>Plutarch</margin> Which **Alcibiades** sufficiently testifies; for when he went into a school and requested from the schoolmaster the ***Iliad*** (which are twenty-four books about the destruction of **Ilium** or the city of **Troy**), and the schoolmaster replied that **Homer's** writings were unknown to him, the said **Alcibiades** gave the lout a slap on the cheek, as if to say: "How shamelessly do you undertake to teach others, when you have not first [read] the Master's books..."

He positions the Iliad and Odyssey not just as poetry, but as essential manuals for moral and political leadership.</summary>

# Preface

<margin>Cicero, in his speech for the poet Archias.</margin>
Those things which should be recounted in all writings—unless you have never read of them—are how Alexander of Macedon,
when he came to the tomb of Achilles at Sigeum, began to cry out with loud and fervent
passion: "O young hero, I consider you blessed because you were
granted **Homer** as a herald <note>original: "Ernhold"; a town crier or official messenger who proclaims a noble's deeds</note> or proclaimer of your praise and virtue,
through whose writing it has come to pass that your memory
and name, along with your body, do not lie buried and forgotten
under this grave and heap of stones." This aforementioned great King had learned Homer's books entirely by
heart and carried them with him everywhere on his travels through field and war (to remind
himself of military actions and counsel);
<margin>Pliny, Book 7.</margin>
at night, he placed them beneath his head pillow. Also, when he
prevailed over King Darius and captured his wagon-fortress, treasures, and jewels, and when
among other things a little chest <note>original: "trütlin"; a small, precious casket or jewelry box</note> of pure gold and gemstones, wonder-
fully costly, was brought before him, his councilors deliberated long and
could think of nothing of such high value that would be worthy of so magnificent
a container. Then Alexander said: "It is fitting and right
that in the most beautiful of chests, the most excellent work ever made
by human understanding (meaning the books of **Homer**) should be
preserved." Likewise, King Archelaus never went to
bed without first reading from the books of Homer; and as soon as he
arose from sleep, he ran back to them with such delight and desire
as a lover hastens to his beloved. He was also accustomed to calling Homer
his sweetheart. I could also recount here many of the most distinguished
teachers of Holy Scripture who occasionally interweave Homer’s verses into
their writings and, through Homeric examples, incite a love for virtue;
also the oldest scribes of Imperial Law, who in more than one place
alone introduce Homer's sayings as testimony. But so that no one
may think my purpose in this preface is to encompass all the praise of
Homer—which can neither be increased by any single tribute nor
diminished by any slander—I will let it rest here and
finally reveal what has moved and encouraged me, a man of modest understanding, toward this
translation: namely, that while through the grace and will
of the Almighty, the immeasurable gifts of the artistic languages, which pre-
viously existed only among the Greeks and Latins, have in our memory
(praise be to God) also reached us Germans. Thereby the German
tongue has reached and grown in elegance, in the true art of speaking and writing,
such that not only the most excellent books of Divine
Scripture, but also all kinds of histories—which in our times have
transpired in wonderfully rare ways—as well as much subtle art,
newly born in our language, have come to light; but also the writings
and inventions of the oldest theologians, philosophers, orators, poets,
and historians, from the idiom in which they spoke, are
translated so diligently and in such great numbers that far
more wisdom, art, and knowledge are contained in the German
than in the Italian tongue, recorded in letters. And thus, the great nation under the sun
is distinguished not only with weapons and triumphs, but also with
wisdom, reason, courtesy, customs, eloquence—in short, with all
well-rounded knowledge.

Kün. Maie."; referring to the King of the Romans, the title used by the Holy Roman Emperor-elect</note>, etc., my commanding lord and patron—first undertaken to translate certain books of **Homer's** *Odyssey* <note>original: "Odyssee Homeri"</note> into German. I sent these to my aforementioned most gracious lord as a recreation <note>original: "ergezligkait"; meaning a pleasant diversion or relief</note> from his business and illness. Subsequently, encouraged and urged by his lordship’s approval, I took heart to translate the entire work of the *Odyssey*—not word for word, but sense-for-sense <note>original: "sinßweiß"; a translation philosophy prioritizing the meaning and narrative flow over a literal, grammatical rendering</note>, as I could most closely and clearly grasp the true meaning according to my small and humble understanding. I have now released it publicly in print, in the good hope that such an edition will provide benefit and pleasure to those who seek pastime in German books and histories. I ask all of them here, if I have not satisfied their judgment in any way, that they might graciously attribute this to my human frailty (for nothing in all the world is perfect) and favor my good intentions and faithful diligence more than my linguistic skill. Thus, if you keep me, **Master Simon Minervius** <note>original: "Simonis Minerii"; the Latinized name of Simon Schaidenreisser</note>, in your best thoughts, it will be a primary incentive for me to also bring to print the greater work of **Homer** regarding the expedition and war for Troy, entitled the *Iliad* <note>original: "Iliada"</note>—which I have now begun to translate <note>original: "transfferieren"</note> and have in hand—as well as several books of **Cicero**, namely the *Paradoxes* <note>original: "Paradoxa"</note> and the *Dream of Scipio* <note>original: "Somnium Scipionis"</note>.

# The Life of **Homer**, drawn from **Herodotus of Halicarnassus**, **Plutarch**, also **Dio Chrysostom**, and others.

Since **Homer**, in all his writings, makes no specific mention of his name, fatherland, or parents, there are consequently many different and conflicting opinions regarding his origin, life, and death, all of which would be fruitless and tedious to recount. **Herodotus of Halicarnassus**, whom I follow in this matter, writes: When the city of **Cyme** <note>original: "Cuma"</note> in Asia was first built and a great many people gathered there, a man of modest status and means named **Melanopus**, from the city of **Magnesia**, settled there with his household and trade. Shortly thereafter, he married the daughter of a citizen of Cyme, with whom he soon had an heir named **Critheis**. Upon his death and that of his wife, the father entrusted Critheis to be raised by a particularly trusted friend, **Cleonax**. While under his care, she secretly became pregnant, which moved Cleonax to such resentment toward Critheis that he sent her away from him to **Smyrna** and placed her with a citizen named **Ismenias**. 

Now, while Critheis—along with other women <note>original: "weißsbilde"; an archaic term for women</note>—ventured out on a journey to a church dedication or festival while heavily pregnant, she went into labor not far from the water or river **Meles** <note>original: "Melites"</note> and brought **Homer** into the world. She named him **Melesigenes**, after the aforementioned river. Once she had recovered from childbirth, she supported herself and her offspring through the hard labor of her hands. She hired herself out to a widely famous schoolmaster or <term>Musico</term> <note>meaning a teacher of the liberal arts, including music and poetry</note> named **Phemius**, whom she served honorably. Eventually, he was so pleased by her appearance and her skill <note>original: "wolfündigkait"</note> that he desired to marry her. She granted his request all the more willingly because he promised to raise Melesigenes as his own natural son. He proved this through his actions, teaching the boy with such diligence that in a short time, Melesigenes not only left all his fellow students far behind in the subtlety of his mind and his artistic poetry and writing, but he also equaled his foster father. After Phemius died, Melesigenes was accepted in his place as the schoolmaster and guardian of the youth, held in great renown by both residents and foreigners.

And since **Smyrna** was a well-known and much-visited merchant city, and many foreigners traveled there for the business of buying and selling, they would visit Melesigenes's school on holidays and diligently listen to his singing. It so happened that **Mentes**, a man of great experience and not unlearned, from **Leucas**, brought several ships to Smyrna to load grain. Having become acquainted with Melesigenes, the young schoolmaster and poet—who had already formed the intention in his mind to write something magnificent and was therefore eager to see many lands and cities—was easily persuaded to leave the school at Smyrna and sail here and there across the sea with Mentes. They traveled as far as **Spain**, then to **Italy** <note>original: "Welschland"</note>, and further to **Ithaca**. There, Melesigenes fell into a severe illness of the eyes (for he naturally had weak vision). While he lay ill at the house of a prominent citizen named **Mentor**, he inquired about what kind of war-leader **Ulysses** <note>Odysseus</note> had been and how many noble deeds he had performed. When his eyes had improved, he moved to **Colophon**, but soon fell back into the previous eye ailment and went completely blind. From this misfortune, the name **Homer** was given to him, for the Greek word *Homerus* sounds in our language much like "blind." After this, Homer turned all his diligence, mind, and understanding to *Carmina* <note>original: "Carmina"; Latin for songs or poems</note> or artistic poetry, with which he earned his maintenance <note>original: "vnderhaltung"</note> by singing in public squares and across the countryside...

It describes his travels with the merchant Mentes, his research into the life of Odysseus in Ithaca, and how he eventually became blind and adopted the name Homer.</summary>

Jupiter holds a general assembly of the gods wherein, at the diligent urging of Minerva, it is unanimously decided that Ulysses <note>the Greek hero Odysseus</note> shall return from the island of Ogygia to his fatherland, Ithaca. Minerva appears to Telemachus in the assumed form of Mentes, king of the Taphians; through whose advice and prompting, Telemachus resolves to travel first to Pylos to see Nestor, and then to King Menelaus in the city of Sparta, in search of his father. And before his departure, he speaks with the Suitors <note>original: "Werbern", those seeking to marry Ulysses's wife, Penelope</note>, ordering them now to leave his house; but since they do not comply, Telemachus goes to bed indignant and troubled.

<margin>
Homer maintains a divine eternal providence (in Latin: *praedestinatio*). The cause of Neptune’s wrath against Ulysses will become apparent from this book and those following—namely, that Ulysses robbed the son of Neptune, the Cyclops, of his eye. See Book 9.

<margin>
Whether there are two kinds of Moors <note>The original "moren" refers to the Ethiopians</note> and how Homer should be understood here can be found in Strabo’s first book.
</margin>

The Greeks who first remained alive after the war for Troy, and who subsequently escaped death and danger on the shipwreck-prone sea, were all living at home. Only Ulysses was held in the cave of the goddess Calypso (who desired him for her lawful husband), far from his land, from his wife and children, against his will. And as the years passed and the time approached in which, by eternal providence, he was to return again to his fatherland and yet endure more war therein, all the gods took pity on his misfortune—except Neptune. He bore an old hatred toward him and always prevented him from his much-desired homecoming, until the aforementioned god went for a time to the far-distant and outermost peoples of the world (listen!), to the Ethiopians or Moors, some of whom dwell toward the sunset and the others toward the sunrise.

<margin>
The Laconians <note>Spartans</note> sacrificed a hundred oxen annually. Sacrifices of a hundred animals of one kind are called a <term>hecatomb</term>.
</margin>

<margin>
Not God, but the sin and wickedness of humans is the cause of our misfortune.
</margin>

<margin>
Orestes was a son of King Agamemnon; he avenged his father’s death and shame and stabbed his adulterous mother. See Book 3.
</margin>

<margin>
* Minerva, a daughter of the almighty god and a goddess of all wisdom, takes up the cause of the wise Ulysses; she prays and frets everywhere on his behalf. By this, it is given to understand that the wise man is never abandoned by wisdom at any time or in any need; indeed, that wisdom alone is an eternal, unchangeable good to its lovers and possessors.
</margin>

While Neptune was there himself, present with special pleasure at the <term>hecatomb</term> <note>original: "hunderthäuptigẽ opffer," a sacrifice of a hundred heads of cattle</note> of fat oxen and sheep, the other gods all gathered in the high heavenly Hall of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>. And when they had sat down, the highest god Jupiter (an almighty father of gods and men) began to speak thus: "Ach, the great injustice! Everything adverse that happens to men on earth is blamed upon us gods by them. They think nothing else than that we are the origin and cause of all evil that happens in the wide world and under the sun, yet they often perish through their own blasphemous deeds and strive for misfortune and evil themselves, from which they might well have been spared through our will. Of this, * Aegisthus the son of Thyestes gives you a clear and undeniable example; he who turned Agamemnon’s wife, Clytemnestra, away from him, and all while Agamemnon lay before Troy, lived with her in unseemly mingling—and above all that, at last, miserably strangled him. Though he was not ignorant that his own destruction would follow from it; for we sent Mercury and had him warned to refrain from that forbidden love and this murder, or else such a blasphemous deed would soon be avenged by Orestes as soon as he came to a manly age and felt the zeal and innate desire for his father’s land. But the warning of Mercury produced nothing fruitful in him, nor could it convert his mind, until he has now paid heavily with his body and life the penalty of the adulterous vice and all his crimes." Upon this spoke * Minerva:

"O dearest father, he died a deserved death, and I wish that all who perform such vices should be granted no other nor better end. I do not pity Aegisthus at all, but the misfortune of poor, blessed Ulysses troubles me; he who stays far from his fatherland, in the middle of the sea, in the house of Calypso, the goddess and daughter of Atlas, with sweet caress..."

# The First Book

<margin>Here and in the following books, it can be understood that among the ancients, the custom was not to sit at tables as we do, but to eat while reclining in beds <note>original: "pettẽ" (beds/couches)</note>, as Valerius Maximus indicates in his second book. <note>Valerius Maximus was a Roman author who wrote about ancient customs and history.</note></margin>
He placed Minerva’s spear against a column or pillar in the armory, where Ulysses’ weapons and armor were kept. She, however, he seated in a royal chair covered with artistically worked tapestry, and sat beside her in a separate seat to inquire about the return of his father. The housekeeper prepared a special table for the guest, reached out the fragrant hand-water in a golden vessel for her to wash her hands over a silver basin. The stewardess brought out food and bread and blessed it for them; likewise, the carvers brought all kinds of meat in bowls, carrying them politely in their hands.

<margin>The luxurious and idle life of the Suitors, as described here, gave rise to the Latin proverb *sponsi Penelopes* <note>original: "spõ si Penelopes" — the suitors of Penelope; a phrase used to describe those who live idly at another's expense.</note>.</margin>
The herald did not delay in pouring the best wine into the golden bowls and cups. Afterward, the Suitors also entered and lay down one after another on the dining couches. They took the hand-water and fell greedily upon the food. The table-servants left no cup empty, and when the meal was finished, they began to sing and dance. The herald quickly handed the singer, Phemius, a sweet-sounding harp to play and perform. Telemachus whispered into the guest's ear, saying: "Guest, do not let the time feel long because of these gluttons. They have no other care than dancing, singing, jumping, and sitting daily at a prepared table, consuming and squandering the property of a man whose bones now lie unburied, rotting in the rain and wind, or perhaps floating in the sea. Should he rise again and come to Ithaca, not one among them would want to earn all the goods he expects. But now they are easily confident, since he has perished. ## Summary of the second book.

Telemachus calls a general assembly / presents his request therein / and after he has received the necessary provisions for the journey from Eurycleia / and a prepared ship together with companions from Minerva / he sets sail from the land.

After this, he stepped forth from the sleeping chamber / carrying a long spear in his hand / two dogs ran behind him / and when he came to the place where a general assembly was gathered / everyone was struck with awe at his divine appearance (with which he had been adorned by Minerva) / they all rose toward him with great reverence / and gave him place to sit in his father’s princely chair / Soon the noble hero Aegyptius / who was now entirely bowed and bent due to his old age / began to speak before the others.

### The Second Book

You men of Ithaca, since the time when the illustrious Prince Ulysses <note>The Roman name for Odysseus, the hero of the epic.</note> departed from here together with others for Troy, not a single gathering of the community has been held until now. What then does this current, exceeding call to assembly mean? Are there perhaps some good new tidings concerning the return of our most dear Ulysses—who is the heart of us all—and our own people? Or have other matters of great importance to the common good been made known, which he wishes to present here to this entire honorable community? For truly, I praise him and consider him a pious, well-meaning man who, when God inspires him with something special and hidden, or sends it through revelation, does not hide it from his fellow citizens, but shares it with all for their salvation and joy. Thus spoke Aegyptius. Telemachus had never before sat in the power and majesty of his father, nor had he ever delivered a speech before the community. Therefore, his heart rightfully swelled with joy because of such great and unusual honor. 

<margin>Pisenor.</margin>
Before him stood the herald Pisenor, holding a royal scepter, which Telemachus received in his hand. He turned toward the aforementioned elder and spoke thus:

<margin>
SPEECH
Telemachus’s Answer.
</margin>
"O elder, you who have called for this assembly: he who did so is not far off and is quite well known to you. For I have done it, and it was not (as you perhaps think) because of any new tidings or good news from my father, nor for the common good, but my own necessity, pain, and double damage have caused and driven me to this. For first, I have lost my dear father,

<margin>A prince is the father of his subjects.</margin>
who was the faithful father and gracious ruler of you all together. Secondly, the most powerful men of the surrounding lands (who all court my lady mother <note>These are the "Suitors," the noblemen pressuring Penelope to remarry so they can seize power in Ithaca.</note>) are consuming my property and wealth. They go in and out of my house daily, eating and drinking the most precious things, squandering what is there; and there is no one who takes my side to defend me. I, as a young, weak orphan, am not able to forbid such things alone. If I had the strength and power, I would not leave unavenged the insolence and pride they display toward my property, nor would I in any way tolerate them burdening me and my house in such an unbearable manner. Since, however (as you just heard), I do not lack the will or spirit, but only the means, I wish to complain of my concern and hardship to all of you, as you are gathered here. 

<margin>An appeal for help.</margin>
You, as the stronger ones and those who are related to me by our common fatherland, do not deign to allow this injustice any longer.

<margin>God punishes not only those who work evil, but also those who do not repel evil when it is within their power.</margin>
Instead, fear the gossip of the surrounding peoples, and above all, fear the wrath of God, so that He, as the most just judge, does not send a heap of misfortune, trouble, and adversity upon you because you left insolence and malice unpunished. This I ask of you by God and by holy justice <note>Original: "hailige gerechtigkeit." This likely refers to Themis, the personification of divine order and the goddess of assemblies.</note>, which gathers, binds, and again dissolves the minds of men. Also, insofar as my father never offended you against what is right, let me enjoy the benefit of that now; punish those who work malice and incite others to it, so that I am not forced to complain to strangers and seek their help." Thus he spoke earnestly, and with a face of anger,

<margin>Antinous rebukes Telemachus’s speech and excuses the Suitors.</margin>
he threw the scepter to the ground, moving all the people to compassion. And while everyone remained silent and no one was daring enough to answer him, Antinous began: "Telemachus, you employ [arrogant words]..."

...you should even faithfully warn and admonish Telemachus, as one would a son, that he must send his mother back to her father’s house. Her father will certainly know how to marry her to someone who pleases him, providing a dowry, the wedding feast, and everything else that a dear father is expected to perform. Indeed, as long as this does not happen, the Suitors will not vacate Telemachus’s house nor cease their pursuit of his mother. They are not so easily turned away; they fear no one, caring neither for Telemachus’s sharp tongue and bold words, nor for your prophecy, which will ultimately be your own downfall. Telemachus’s paternal inheritance and goods will be consumed all the more, the longer we all wait for Penelope’s marriage, as each of us hopes to be the one chosen.

To this, the <margin>Telemachus's request</margin> wise Telemachus replied: "Eurymachus, and you other noble Suitors. I will no longer beg you to cease this injustice, which is now known to all gods and men. I only ask now—for which purpose I hold this assembly—that you provide me with a swift ship and twenty companions. With these, I intend to sail to Pylos and Sparta to discover the truth of my father’s situation, whether he is alive or dead. If I hear any hope of his life and return, wandering for an entire year after him shall be neither too long nor too difficult for me. But as soon as I truly learn that he is no longer living, I will return home immediately, raise a tomb for him, and then kindly persuade my mother to bind herself in marriage to another man." Having spoken thus, he sat down.

Mentor, an old companion and friend of Ulysses—to whom Ulysses, when he wished to depart for Troy, entrusted all his household, wife, child, and goods, so that the entire household looked up to him with great respect—stood up and spoke: 
<margin>The Speech of Mentor <note>original: "ORATIO Mentoris"</note></margin>
"Hear me, you Ithacans! From now on, no king or ruling lord should be kind, merciful, just, or gracious, but rather harsh and unkind. For Ulysses, despite his fatherly goodness, love, and justice toward his subjects, has earned nothing more than to be so quickly forgotten; no one shows any help or support to his son in exchange for the many benefits received. I do not begrudge the Suitors their feasting and drinking; they do so at the risk of their own bodies and lives. What vexes me, however, is that there are so many of you, and you all sit there, keeping silent, looking on as if through your fingers <note>original: "durch die finger zü" — a German idiom meaning to look the other way or ignore something obvious.</note> while the Suitors so wastefully squander Ulysses’s goods."

<margin>Liocrites’s answer</margin> 
Liocrites answered: "Mentor, you old grumbler and fool, what have you just said? Do you bid us abandon our purpose and depart? It would be far too difficult, not only for you but even for Ulysses (if it were possible for him to return home), to drive us from the food in this courtyard. Even his wife, who longs for him so greatly, would experience little joy if she had to see with her own eyes how he, as a lone man, was struck down and slain by so many of us strong and hardy men. Therefore, you have spoken wrongly. You of the common people may each return to your business; let not Mentor’s speech lead you astray. Alitherses and Mentor have always been good friends and companions of Ulysses. Therefore, they advise Telemachus to go searching for his father. But I do not doubt that he will [soon]...

## The Second Book

Soon a message arrived, by which this journey was postponed. After this speech, he dismissed the assembly, and everyone went to their own home. The Suitors betook themselves, as before, to Ulysses’s <note>The Greek hero Odysseus, known in this text by his Latin name</note> court. Telemachus walked along the seashore, washed his hands, and prayed to Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom, Athena</note> thus:

<margin>PRAYER: Telemachus’s prayer to his patroness Minerva.</margin>
> O goddess, you who appeared to me yesterday in the assumed form of a guest and advised me to board a ship to seek my father, who has been abroad for a long time. I pray you, hear my prayer and be helpful, so that the arrogant, faithless Suitors do not prevent or hinder me in my undertaking.

<margin>Minerva’s answer and comfort.</margin>
Minerva took upon herself the form of the body and the voice of <term>Mentor</term> <note>A loyal friend of Ulysses; Minerva often disguises herself as him to provide advice</note> and answered thus: "Telemachus, if you wish to be undaunted and hardworking, and to seek your dear, knightly father with boldness and deeds, then you will easily complete the task you have before you. Neither the effort nor the way will cause you regret. But if you did not have the blood and nature of Ulysses within you, your undertaking would become far too difficult for you."

<margin>Proverb: Children do not always take after their parents.</margin>
> For few are born like their noble fathers,
> The greater part are always far worse.
<note>Original Latin: "Pauci nam similes patribus nascuntur honestis, Peiores longe ueniunt pars maxima semper."</note>

Children rarely take after their parents; the greater part fall away from the lineage, and very few are found who walk in the footsteps of their parents, and even fewer who surpass their fathers in piety and virtue. But of you—to whom not only the goods, but also the spirit and the virtue of your father Ulysses have been bequeathed—I have no doubt that you will perform great, glorious, and knightly deeds. Do not let the <term>practick</term> <note>Deceptive schemes or political intrigues</note> and malice of the Suitors trouble you at all; they are unwise, unjust people, and do not recognize that their destruction follows so closely at their heels. In me, you shall have a faithful helper. I will prepare a ship for us and be a companion to you wherever you sail. For now, go home in haste and speak with the Suitors. Prepare yourself for the journey with necessary food; put flour in leather sacks, and wine in bottles and jars. Meanwhile, I will not be idle and will round up several willing companions to keep us company. There are many new, well-maintained ships on the shore; from all of them, I will choose the best, equip it, and set out upon the sea. Telemachus was not slow; following this exhortation from the goddess, he hurried into the city and found the shameless Suitors in the court, eating and drinking.

<margin>Antinous to Telemachus.</margin>
Antinous went toward him, offering his hand and saying: "Eloquent Telemachus, overcome your anger; think no ill of us, but eat and drink and be of good cheer, as you were with us before. <margin>Telemachus’s Answer.</margin>
Telemachus answered: "I acknowledge your offer, but it is not fitting for me, a simple man, to keep much company or to share food and drink with you bold and proud men. You have consumed enough of my wealth until now, while I was still a minor and small, and I have endured it. But now that I..."

### Homer’s Odyssey

Now that I have come of age, I will follow the counsel of the wise. From their instruction and teaching, I have gathered such heart that I will endeavor, either here or at Pylos, to bring misfortune upon you. I have a journey before me, and I hope it will not fail me entirely. With these words, he snatched his hand from the hand of Antinous <note>The leader of the Suitors</note>. Meanwhile, the other Suitors were busy eating and drinking; some of them secretly grumbled and mocked Telemachus’s words.

<margin>The Suitors' mocking speech.</margin>
One prominent man said: "Telemachus has sworn our death; therefore he will not remain here longer, but will rouse many helpers from Pylos and Sparta against us."

<margin>Ephyra (as Strabo <note>A famous Greek geographer</note> writes) is a city in Thessaly, fertile in grain, but it bears many deadly poisons.</margin>
"Or perhaps he will even travel to Ephyra to buy poison there, to poison us in our food or drink." Another spoke mockingly: "You do not understand the matter rightly; I only fear he may travel to join his father and never return, leaving us the trouble of seizing, distributing, and consuming his goods among ourselves." They spoke such mocking words within Telemachus's hearing.

Telemachus went into the treasury, where gold and all kinds of bronze were piled, along with much clothing in chests, many fragrant waters, and many jars of oil on one side. On the other side lay large barrels filled with precious wine, stacked from the floor to the ceiling.

<margin>Euryclea.</margin>
Beside the wine barrels sat Euryclea <note>Ulysses's old nurse and a trusted servant</note> nearly day and night without ceasing, filling and cleaning the barrels, keeping a diligent watch so that no harm should come to them.

<margin>Telemachus. Euryclea.</margin>
Telemachus spoke to the aforementioned housekeeper, saying: "Dear little mother, you shall fill twelve jars for me with the best and sweetest wine, and seal them well. In addition, pack twenty measures <note>The original uses 'Schaf,' a historical unit of volume for grain</note> of rye flour. For tomorrow morning or evening, when the sun sets and my mother has gone to bed, I will depart from here for Sparta and Pylos to inquire after my father."

<margin>Euryclea.</margin>
Euryclea was terrified by these words, began to weep bitterly, and said: "O dearest son, what are you undertaking? Where do you intend to go? Will you travel so alone and in vain to far-off lands? Your father has long since perished in foreign parts, and if you now journey after him, the Suitors will hatch a plot against us, to waylay you on the road, murder you, and seize your possessions here by force. Therefore, you should think better of it and remain here with us; for there is no need for you to wander amidst the dangers which are unspeakably great upon the sea."

<margin>Telemachus.</margin>
Telemachus answered: "Dear little mother, be untroubled; my undertaking does not happen without the will of the almighty gods. Only promise me that you will not reveal a single word of my departure—which I have trusted to you in secret—to my mother before the eleventh or twelfth day, so that she does not cry her eyes out and mar her tender face with tears." She soon swore a faithful oath to him, filled several jars with wine, and packed the flour into sacks, as necessity required and as she had been commanded. Telemachus went down again with the intention of speaking with the Suitors. ### Summary of the third book.

Nestor honorably receives the wandering guests Telemachus and **Minerva** <note>The Roman name for the goddess Athena, who continues to guide Telemachus in the guise of his friend Mentor.</note>; he tells them what the Greeks endured on their journey home from **Troy** <note>original: "Troia."</note>; in turn, he asks Telemachus about the state of his household and the **Suitors** <note>original: "Werber"; the men pressuring Telemachus's mother, Penelope, to remarry.</note> seeking his mother’s hand. And when he realizes that Minerva is present in human form visiting his home, he performs a costly sacrifice to her, gives Telemachus rich gifts, and sends him toward **Sparta** <note>original: "Spartha."</note> with a horse-drawn carriage and all necessities, sending his son Pisistratus with him. At nightfall they arrive at Pheris and stay with Diocles, the son of Ortilochus.

And if I were to tell you everything in succession that happened to us before Troy (where then the strongest—Ajax, Achilles, Patroclus, and my dearest son Antilochus, along with many a proud hero—perished), and also what befell us on the wandering journey home, I would need more than five whole years for it. You would also, before you had heard me out, return sadly to your homeland. And before all others, Menelaus stood up; he expressed his gratitude to everyone for the support and help they had provided and gave leave for each of us to return to our homelands. This did not please his brother Agamemnon, for his counsel and opinion was that a general sacrifice should first be performed, hoping thereby to appease the angry goddess Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom and war, who was often angry with the Greeks during their return.</note>. And because the two brothers, as the two highest heads of the army, were against one another and quarreled with words, the common people also grumbled among themselves and thus became divided. I and Diomedes, with our followers and ships, hurried toward Lesbos. There we waited until Menelaus arrived much later, and we consulted whether we should sail above or below Chios. Stratius and Echephron led the sacrifice; Arethus quickly reached out a bright pouring-basin <note>original: "gießbeck"</note> for the washing of hands; Thrasymedes carried the battle-axe in his hand; Perseus held the wooden bowl to catch the blood <note>original: "schweiß" — literally "sweat," a traditional Germanic hunting term for blood</note> therein.

<margin>The custom of sacrificing to Minerva.</margin>

When all this had been done and the grains were offered, Thrasymedes immediately struck with the axe, cutting through the neck-tendons <note>original: "flachssadern" — literally "flaxen-veins," referring to the sinews</note> of the cow so that she fell. The daughters and daughters-in-law of Nestor,

and his chaste wife Eurydice, wailed (as was the custom) and quickly hoisted the sacrifice from the earth by all four legs, holding it aloft. When no more life was felt and the limbs had all grown cold, they removed the entrails and burned them, made many portions, and cooked some; the fat and the best parts they put on a long spit, turned it over the fire, and roasted it.

<margin>Polycasta, Nestor’s daughter.</margin>
Afterward came the beautiful Polycasta, the youngest of all Nestor’s daughters; she washed the naked body of Telemachus with warm water and anointed him with fragrant oil, and put a new tunic and cloak upon him. Telemachus, thus cleansed, shone like a godly angel <note>original: "Gott der Engel"</note>; he sat beside Nestor at the table; they ate the roast and drank the well-flavored wine with it. And when they were satisfied, Nestor began and spoke: "Dear sons, go now, prepare the wagon and lead the horses to it, so that Telemachus may journey away upon it."

## Summary of the fourth book.
<note>original: "Argumentum"</note>

Telemachus and Pisistratus are received in a friendly manner at the royal court of Menelaus; after many offerings of discipline and honor, Telemachus tells the King how things stand within his father’s household, why he has undertaken such a long journey, and how he came to be there. Menelaus informs him which Greeks came home safely from the Trojan War and which perished on the dangerous sea. Likewise, how he learned from the prophecy of Proteus, the sea god <note>original: "mörrische gots"</note>, that his brother <note>Agamemnon</note> was miserably murdered by Orestes with the help of his unfaithful wife, and that the patient Ulysses is being held by the lady Calypso. While Ulysses is thus absent, the suitors in the house of Ulysses plot how they might strike down and eliminate Telemachus on his journey home. Minerva disguises herself in the form of Ipthime (who was a sister of Penelope), appears to Penelope, and comforts her with the announcement of the soon-to-be return of her dearest son Telemachus.

<margin>Lacedaemon or Lacedaemonia was the land of King Menelaus; it had a hundred cities, including the capital also called Lacedaemon or Sparta; in our times that same region is called Morea <note>A medieval name for the Peloponnese peninsula.</note></margin>
As soon as Telemachus and Pisistratus had reached the fish-rich and well-known royal Lacedaemon, they made their way straight to the court of Menelaus, who at that time was holding a great banquet and wedding feast. For he was just then preparing to send his daughter to the son of Achilles (as he had promised her to him in the field camp before Troy) with horses and wagons into the city 
<margin>* The Myrmidons were people of Greece over whom Achilles ruled.</margin>
* of the Myrmidons. Also, his youngest son—named Megapenthes, born not of Helen (who never bore a male child) but of a captured servant-girl—had taken the daughter of Prince Alector as his lawful wife and had recently brought her home from Sparta. For this reason, the guests sat in the wide royal hall, eating, drinking, dancing, and leaping with joy. The divine poet <note>The author, Homer</note> sang an artistic poem to the sweet sound of the harps. Telemachus and Pisistratus remained in the forecourt, standing still beside their horses. And as soon as Etoneus, the diligent servant of Menelaus, caught sight of them, he said to him...

### Summary of the fifth book.

Jupiter holds the second assembly of the heavenly gods, sends Mercury to Lady Calypso with orders not to detain Ulysses <note>The Greek hero Odysseus.</note> any longer; Calypso obeys and sends Ulysses on his way. When he had sailed for eighteen days, the angry god Neptune sees him, overturns and smashes his ship; Ino gives him a plank from the ship, upon which he swims to land, and after much misfortune, arrives in the region of the Phaeacians <note>Original: "Pheacam".</note>.

# The Fifth Book.

<margin>Assembled council of the gods.</margin>
Dawn rose during this time, bringing forth the heavenly light for gods and men; the gods gathered in a great crowd at the court of the highest ruler, Jove <note>Jupiter or Zeus.</note>. Ulysses did not delay; he nimbly cut down twenty trunks or trees, trimmed them, and planed them according to the line. Calypso also helped, and he bored through each tree with the auger or drill, joining and fastening them to each other with iron nails. Afterward, he planked the floor, prepared the mast, and likewise the oars. When the raft was ready on the shore on the fourth day and had been pulled completely to the water, Calypso came and brought several linens for sails. On the fifth day, she sent him (as he was now ready to depart) new, white-washed shirts, a skin with water, another with wine, and all kinds of food. She also granted him a lucky, gentle wind.

<margin>Ulysses’ exclamation <note>original Latin: "Vlyssis exclamatio"</note>.</margin>
Ulysses’ entire body and heart grew cold with fear and anguish; he sighed and cried out loudly, saying: "O, what a bitter misfortune now stands before my eyes! I fear the prophecy of the goddess Calypso will come all too true, who told me I must still suffer much and endure many wild struggles and dangers before I reach the soil of my fatherland. O, how miserable I am; I see my misfortune before me. O, many times blessed are those Greeks whose lot it was to end their lives gallantly before the high city walls of Troy. O Achilles, you strongest hero of all the Greeks, why did the Trojans not slay me with their spears when they surrounded me alongside you? Then my body, like yours, would have been honorably mourned by the Greeks and buried in the earth; my name would have been inscribed for eternal memory and praised by those to come. But now I must die a terrifying and un-knightly death <note>original: "ritterlichē," meaning knightly; however, the context suggests Ulysses views drowning as an "un-knightly" or ignoble end compared to dying in battle</note>."

And as he was crying out thus, making many vain complaints, behold, a great stream of water and a wave shot forth, striking Ulysses along with the rudder into the sea. It pushed the ship or raft over and over, so that the raft drifted upon the sea without a pilot. Ulysses struggled with all his might so that he might survive the danger of imminent death this time; and although he was nearly weighed down by the heavy cloak <note>original: "rock"</note> that the goddess Calypso had given him, he finally swam out, dripping all over. He spat out much of the salt water that had gone into him, yet in such distress and anguish, he did not forget his raft at all. Instead, as it had drifted toward land, Ulysses sat upon it again, waiting to see where the winds would drive him.

<margin>Leucothea, a daughter of King Cadmus; as she drowned herself, she was thereafter called upon and honored as a goddess of the sea.</margin>
Leucothea, a daughter of Cadmus and now a goddess and inhabitant of the sea, saw Ulysses from afar, sailing there, blown and driven back and forth by the contrary winds. She was moved with pity for him and, disguising herself in the form of a kingfisher <note>original: "eisvogel," literally an ice-bird or halcyon</note>, she flew to him. Sitting upon the raft, she spoke: "You wretched Ulysses, how hatefully the god Neptune persecutes and pursues you, inflicting much evil upon you; yet he shall not be able to destroy you entirely. But follow me: throw your garment from you, abandon the raft, and take this veil <note>original: "pråt," likely referring to a protective cloth or headband</note>. Lay yourself upon it at full length with your chest, and paddle with your arms, and thus swim to the land of Phaeacia, where safety shall meet you. And when you have arrived there and are delivered, take the veil and throw it back into the sea." After this speech, she reached him a veil, then hid herself again in the water like a kingfisher.

### The Argument <note>original: "Argumentum," a standard term in early modern books for a plot summary at the start of a chapter.</note> of the sixth book.

Minerva appears in a dream to the daughter of King Alcinous named Nausicaa / she prophesies to her how she will shortly be married / and therefore urges her to travel out to the nearest flowing water / to wash all the clothing and garments for her fast-approaching wedding. Nausicaa follows the encouragement or inspiration / carries out a laundry / and while the clothing dries / she begins to sing and play with her maidservants / by which Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> (who was sleeping nearby) is awakened / he falls submissively and pleadingly at the feet of the royal daughter / by whom he is refreshed with food and drink / also presented with a garment / and receives instructions on where he should go and how he should conduct himself.

Minerva <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena.</note> / hurried to the people called Phaeacians / who in ancient times had their residence in the wide and high-situated region of Hyperia / not far from the district of the proud and inhuman one-eyed Cyclopes or Giants. But as they were attacked by them with war on several occasions / they—for the sake of peace / as the weaker must give place and room to the powerful—departed / and came with their King Nausithous <note>original: "Nausicoo"</note> into the island of Scheria / and settled there /

<margin>Minerva speaks to Nausicaa.</margin>
O Nausicaa, why does your mother keep you so heedless / why do you let your young and joyful days be so lazily worn away? You have now grown to a marriageable age / and it is time that you should be wed / and it would be fitting that you first enjoy the world in joy / with costly, fine clothing / and beautiful shifts / to put them on / and to give a portion as gifts / to those who woo you. For whichever maiden is desired in honor by many noble suitors / she gains a good reputation above and beyond others / and brings her parents satisfaction and joy. I will prophesy to you / you will not remain single long / but shall shortly be married to a prominent and excellent lord. Therefore let us / as soon as it is day, hold a washing / to wash all the garments clean and pure for the coming wedding joy / for which I will help / and will provide a companion to go to the water. Only pray your dear lord father / that he may order a wagon for us / at an early hour / upon which we may load all the garments and veils trimmed with gold / and drive them out. It would not befit you as a King's daughter / to go out on foot. Furthermore, it is a long way. Thus speaking, the blue-eyed goddess departed again toward heaven / into the eternal, peaceful dwelling of the gods / where no violence of the

### Book Six

<margin>Simile.</margin>
<margin>Ulysses goes naked to the young women.</margin>
...he came forth from the thicket, tearing a thick branch from the tree with his strong arm to cover his nakedness. Like a brave lion driven by the necessity of hunger, panting and with burning eyes, steps fiercely from his cave and falls impetuously upon the cattle—so hunger drove Ulysses to present himself, naked and bare, before the eyes of the young women, who were immeasurably terrified of him. For he was still all unclean from the sea-water, sand, and mud. Therefore they ran away from him, one here, the others there, seeking how they might hide. Only the young Queen <note>Nausicaa is a princess, but the German text refers to her here as "Künigin" (Queen).</note> Nausicaa was given such a bold heart by the goddess Minerva that she did not flee like the others, but stood still before Ulysses. Ulysses first doubted whether he should fall at her feet or address her with humble, gentle words. And after long consideration, he decided in his mind to petition her while standing at a distance, so that she might deign to show him the nearest city and perhaps gift him with some clothing. Therefore he addressed her, speaking with clever and modest words as follows.

<margin>The SPEECH of Ulysses to Nausicaa. <note>original: "ORATIO Vlyſſis zü Nauſicaam"</note></margin>
<margin>Diana, daughter of Jove <note>original: "Jovis"</note>, a goddess of the hunt.</margin>
<margin>The parents' pride, joy, and delight above all.</margin>
> O maiden, in truth I consider you not a mortal, but much more a heavenly creature; you also resemble in stature, nature, and form the powerful goddess of the woods and daughter of Jove, named Diana. But if you are indeed a human, then your parents are to be praised as manifoldly blessed for having born such noble fruit <note>A metaphor for a child.</note> and seeing you daily before their eyes. And blessed above all men is he who shall lead you into his house and bed as a wedded spouse. It seems to me, and it is true, that in all my days no more lovely or honorable woman has appeared before my eyes. And I believe surely that you were prefigured and signified to me by the palm tree which I recently saw beside the altar of Apollo <note>Ulysses refers to a famous sacred palm tree on the island of Delos.</note>; for just as I then wondered for a long time how such a beautiful, straight fruit could grow upon the earth, so now, O feminine image, I am frightened, I tremble, and I consider myself unworthy to fall down at your knees to touch them with my hands—for I am indeed a sorrowful and unlucky man. Yesterday ten days have passed since I sailed from the island of Ogygia, and the storms and fury of the winds have beaten me to and fro upon the sea without ceasing, breaking and shattering my raft, until at last God led me here—perhaps so that I should suffer even more adversity in this place. I cannot think that there is yet an end to my misfortune.

<margin>Ulysses’ prayer.</margin>
> Therefore, O Queen, since God has brought me to this land after so many accidents and suffered dangers, and you are the first person I see here, my first plea to you is that you would show mercy toward me and show me the right way to the nearest city; also, if you have an old garment to spare anywhere, that you would deign to gift it to me.

<margin>Ulysses’ wish:</margin>
> For this, noble maiden, I
> Wish you from the gods what you desire.

<note>original Latin: "Non est in rebus melius seu dulcius usquam, / Quam thalami pariter concordia sancta pudici."</note>

<margin>Nausicaa's answer. God gives and takes wealth.</margin>
To this Nausicaa spoke: "O guest, the highest God divides riches among the good and the evil; He gives and takes them according to His divine pleasure. I do not doubt that you once held honor, money, and goods from God; since He has now withdrawn them and sent you adversity, you should, as a wise, brave, and high-minded man (as I judge and perceive you to be), bear the will of God with patience. That which you have asked of me, and even more, shall be granted to you. For I will not only give you clothing, but also everything that a poor, needy man should and may ask for. Furthermore, I will show you the city of this place and tell you the names of its inhabitants. The people of this region are called the <term>Phaeacians<note>In Greek mythology, the Phaeacians were a gifted seafaring people who lived on the island of Scheria; they were famous for their hospitality and their magical, self-steering ships.</note></term>, and I am a daughter of King Alcinous, who governs the people in peace through virtue and justice." Speaking thus, she turned toward her maidens and said:

<margin>Nausicaa to her court maidens</margin>
"You servants, stand still! Why do you run? From whom do you flee? Have you never seen a man before? He is no wild man, nor does he bring any enmity; rather, he comes as a guest who has lost his way and knows not where to go. It is only right that we receive him, since the poor, the wretched, and the strangers are especially commended to the protection of Almighty God—so much so, that He will manifoldly reward everything done for them."

<margin>Strangers in misery are under God's protection. Hospitality is a brief thing, but like a great gift. <note>original: "Hospitium res brevis, sed magni muneris instar"</note> Providing lodging is an acceptable good deed.</margin>
Providing hospitality is a fleeting but lovely and acceptable thing; it is counted as a great gift and a good deed. Therefore, give this guest food and drink, and when he is satisfied, lead him to the water to wash himself. The servants rose quickly and exhorted one another; they led Ulysses to a quiet spot by the river and laid out a shirt and a robe for him on the bank. They also gave him a small flask full of fragrant oil, so that he might anoint himself after his bath.

<margin>Ulysses' speech to the young women.</margin>
Ulysses said to them: "You young women, withdraw for a short while to another place until I have washed my body and anointed myself with the oil (which truly has not touched me for a long time). I will by no means wash in your presence, for I am rightly ashamed to fully uncover my body before such beautiful maidens." Thus he spoke; they stepped away and went back to Nausicaa to tell her this.

<margin>Ulysses' appearance.</margin>
When Ulysses had washed away the uncleanness and anointed his body and head, he put on the clothes that Nausicaa had given him. In them, he appeared much more handsome and distinguished than before. His hair was no different to look upon than if a silk-worker or embroiderer had mixed and stitched together pure drawn gold and silver. With such a radiant appearance, he stepped up from the riverbank. The young Queen Nausicaa was filled with great wonder at his beauty.

# The Sixth Book

<margin>A Simile.</margin>
<margin>Ulysses goes naked to the maidens.</margin>
He came forth from the thicket, and with his strong arm, he broke a thick branch from a tree to create a leafy bunch with which to cover his nakedness. Like a brave lion driven by the pangs of hunger, huffing and with burning eyes, he steps grimly out from his cave and falls impetuously upon the cattle. So did hunger drive Ulysses to present himself, naked and bare, before the eyes of the young maidens, who were beyond measure terrified of him. For he was still covered in filth from the sea, water, sand, and mud. Therefore, they ran away from him, some here and others there, seeking how they might hide themselves. Only to the young Queen Nausicaa did the goddess Minerva give such a bold heart that she did not flee like the others, but stood still facing Ulysses. Ulysses hesitated at first, wondering whether he should fall at her feet or address her with humble, gentle words. And after long consideration, he resolved in his mind to stand at a distance and beg her to show him the nearest city and to deign to gift him with some clothing. Therefore, he addressed her with clever, modest words, speaking thus:

<margin>SPEECH of Ulysses to Nausicaa.</margin>
<margin>Diana, daughter of Jove, a goddess of graceful stature.</margin>
<margin>The ornament, joy, and delight of parents on earth.</margin>
> O maiden, in truth I regard you not as a mortal, but much more as a heavenly creature; you resemble in your graceful stature, nature, and form the powerful goddess of the woods and daughter of Jove <note>original: "Iouis"; Jove is another name for Jupiter or Zeus, the king of the gods.</note>, called Diana <note>The Roman name for Artemis, goddess of the hunt, known for her tall and graceful bearing.</note>. But if you are indeed a human, then your parents are to be praised as manifoldly blessed for having borne such noble fruit and seeing you daily before their eyes. Blessed above all men is he who shall lead you into his house and marriage bed as a wedded spouse. It seems to me, and it is true, that in all my life no more lovely or honorable woman has ever appeared before my eyes. And I surely believe that you were prefigured and signified to me by the palm tree that I recently saw beside the altar of Apollo <note>The Greek god of light, music, and prophecy.</note>; for just as I then marveled for a long time at how such a beautiful, straight growth could spring from the earth, so now, O feminine image, I am terrified. I tremble and deem myself unworthy to fall at your knees and touch them with my hands, for I am a truly sorrowful and unfortunate man. Yesterday, the tenth day passed since I have been traveling upon the sea without ceasing, day and night. For after I sailed from the island of Ogygia <note>The mythical island where the nymph Calypso held Ulysses captive for seven years.</note>, the storms and the violence of the winds have driven me hither and thither upon the sea, breaking and shattering my raft, until at last God led me here—perhaps so that I might suffer even more adversity in this place. I cannot imagine that there will ever be an end to my misfortune.

<margin>Ulysses’ prayer.</margin>
> Therefore, O Queen, since God has brought me to this land after so many accidents and endured perils, and you are the first person I see herein, my first plea to you is that you would exercise mercy toward me and show me the right way to the nearest city; also, if you have an extra old garment anywhere, that you would deign to bestow it upon me.

<margin>Ulysses’ wish.</margin>
> For this, noble maiden, I
> Wish you from the gods all you desire.

<note>original: "Hospitium res brevis, sed magni muneris instar"</note>

"It is only right that we take him in, for the poor, the wretched, and the stranger are especially commended to the care of Almighty God. Thus, He will manifoldly repay everything done for them. Hospitality is a fleeting but dear and pleasant thing; it is counted as a great gift and a good deed. Therefore, give this guest food and drink, and when he is satisfied, lead him to the water to wash himself there." The servants stood up quickly, and encouraging one another, they led Ulysses to a quiet spot by the river. They laid a shirt and a coat for him on the bank and gave him a small flask full of fragrant oil, so that he might anoint himself after his bath.

<margin>
Ulysses’ speech to the maidens.
</margin>

Ulysses spoke to them: "You young maidens, withdraw for a short while to another place until I have washed my body and anointed it with the oil (which truly has not touched me for a long time). I will in no way wash in your presence, for I am not without reason ashamed to completely uncover my body before such beautiful maidens."

<margin>
Ulysses’ appearance.
</margin>

As he spoke, they stepped away and went back to Nausicaa to tell her this. When Ulysses had washed away the filth and anointed his body and head, he put on the clothes that Nausicaa had given him. In them, he appeared much more handsome and distinguished than before; his hair was to be looked upon as if a silk-worker or embroiderer had mixed and stitched together pure drawn gold and silver. With such a shining appearance, he stepped up from the shore. The young Queen Nausicaa was filled with great wonder at his beauty.
