# The Seventh Book

->four walkways enclosed on four sides, abutting the city wall.<-

Among the ancients, the most famous and wonderful pleasure gardens counted and primarily named are the Gardens of the Hesperides in the Canaries, the garden of Alcinous in the land of Scheria (which in our day is called Corfu), and the garden of Adonis. Read Pliny, Book 19, Chapter 4. <note>Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History* was a widely used source in the Renaissance for documenting the wonders of the natural world.</note>

In this place, strange and diverse branches were grafted, as well as fruitful pears, apples, pomegranates, olives, and other fruit trees, bearing fruit one after another in both winter and summer—the very sweetest fruits, namely figs, olives, and the like. There also grew most delightful grapevines, so placed and directed toward the sun that while the grapes were being harvested in one place, they were ripening in another; in a third place they were still hard, and in a fourth they were just beginning to bloom, so that ripe grapes could be found at every time of year. In the aforementioned pleasure garden, two noble, vigorous springs arise: one moistens and waters the entire garden, the other flows into the castle beneath the hall, traveling through pipes up into the chambers and rooms, then falls back down again and is distributed throughout the entire city, from which the citizens receive an abundance of water. Such excellent gifts and gods, as you have just heard, were in the house of Alcinous. Ulysses could not marvel at them enough. After a long while, he went into the hall and found the most prominent of the nobility sitting with the King, making offerings to the god Mercury; no one saw Ulysses. But he saw them all. For, as said before, Minerva had surrounded him with a great mist and made him invisible. <margin>Ulysses falls at the Queen's feet.</margin> But when he fell at the feet of Queen Arete, the mist vanished from him. The Queen and all the others, seeing a man appear so suddenly before their eyes, were terrified and their hearts were filled with shock. <margin>Ulysses’ prayer to the Queen.</margin> Ulysses, however, lying at the feet of the Queen, prayed, saying: "Arete, daughter of the blessed Rexenor. I, who have suffered and experienced much adversity, appear here before you, before your lord, the King, and the nobility, in the highest humility. First, I wish for you all collectively that the merciful God may graciously grant you much wealth, health, long life, high dignity, honor, and glory, as well as many beautiful, well-bred children who may succeed you. Thereafter, I pray specifically to you, O Arete, that you might deign to grant me your help, so that I—who have now wandered for a long time and suffer much adversity—may be able to return to my fatherland." Speaking thus, he stood up and sat down in the ashes by the fire. Everyone remained silent, reflecting. <margin>Ethineus, a prominent man among the Phaeacian people.</margin> Then Ethineus <note>This refers to Echeneus, the eldest and most eloquent of the Phaeacian lords.</note> began to speak, he who was the eldest, the most eloquent, and the most experienced among them. He spoke thus: "Alcinous, it is not fitting for you to let the guest sit in the ashes and filth by the hearth; let a silver chair be brought to him, and command your maidservants to bring wine, <margin>Jupiter the Hospitable. <note>original: "Iuppiter hoſpitalis." This refers to the Greek concept of Xenia, protected by Zeus/Jupiter.</note></margin> to sacrifice to the highest god, Jove, who is merciful to guests and the modest. Beyond all this, command the housekeeper to prepare a supper for the guest." <margin>Laodamas, son of Alcinous.</margin> Upon this exhortation, Alcinous took Ulysses by the hand, led him, and seated him upon a silver chair, commanding his dearest son, Laodamas, to sit near him.

### The Seventh Book

<margin>Ulysses would rather die in his homeland than live immortally in a foreign land with Calypso.</margin>
God shattered my ship with a thunderbolt in the middle of the sea, and all my companions were drowned; I alone grabbed the hull of the ship with my hands. I drifted upon the sea for nine whole days and nights, until on the tenth night, after suffering that shipwreck, the gods led me to the aforementioned island of Ogygia. There the goddess <note>Calypso, a nymph who detained Ulysses for seven years.</note> received me willingly, diligently maintained me, and loved me dearly. She even wished to make me immortal, unchanging, and eternally young, if I would have renounced my fatherland and stayed with her. But I could never bring myself to agree to this in my mind; indeed, during the seven years I was with her, not a day passed in which I did not soak and dampen with tears my face and the garments with which Calypso had gifted me.

<margin>Ulysses remained in Calypso's company until the eighth year.</margin>
And when the eighth year after the conquest of Troy arrived, Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note> sent a message to the aforementioned goddess, commanding her not to detain me any longer. Moved by this command and decree, she herself exhorted me to return home and gifted me a ship with all its tackle; she also sent it off from the shore with good fortune, well-laden with grain, wine, and clothes. On the eighteenth day, the mountains of your region and land appeared from afar, at which I, a sorrowful man, was gladdened and took heart again.

However, Neptune <note>The Roman name for Poseidon, the sea god who was angry with Ulysses.</note> soon spoiled this joy for me and sent contrary winds, raised the sea, and shattered my craft, so that I, a shipwrecked man, swam in the sea until I reached your land. There, the waves of the water drove me once more between great rocks not far from the shore; I swam through them with great difficulty and finally came to a flowing river. As night fell with force, I walked along the river, gathered brush and leaves together, and rested there beneath the shrubs and trees until God poured a deep sleep over me. At the time of the sun’s rising, that sweet sleep left me. When I awoke, I saw your daughter’s servants running and playing in the grass, among whom your daughter shone just as the sun shines over all other stars.

I, being older and more sensible, called primarily upon her, the most beautiful one; for had I asked the younger ones, it would have been in vain, for the reason that there is very little understanding in young people.

### Homer’s Odyssey

I interpret everything for the best, excluding anything that happens improperly. <margin>Virtue is worth more than anything else.</margin>
<margin>Alcinous offers his daughter to the foreign guest Ulysses.</margin>
The most eloquent Saint Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379 AD), who wrote a famous treatise on how Christians should read Greek literature.</note>, in his small book on the reading of the books of the Heathens, writes how he heard from an excellent man that the entire work or poetry of Homer is nothing other than a song of praise and an extolling of virtue. This reveals itself everywhere, but especially here, where Homer brings in the shipwrecked Ulysses, naked and bare of clothing, but so adorned with virtue that all those present blush with shame before him, leave their food, and turn all their eyes toward him alone, desiring of the gods to be like Ulysses. That same highly esteemed man also said that when he read this passage <note>original: "locum"</note> in this book of Homer, or heard it read, he felt in his heart as if he heard Homer crying out and shouting with a loud voice: "O you humans, direct your cares toward virtue, which swims out with the shipwrecked and makes the naked, bare, and poor Ulysses so worthy and pleasant among the blessed, rich Phaeacians," etc.

And therefore, if your desire is nothing other than to see your wife, child, and fatherland again, I will nonetheless be helpful to you in this and arrange your homecoming—so that you may know it—as follows: Tomorrow, while you are still lying in bed and sleeping, the Phaeacians, to whom I have commanded this, will take note of the weather. Afterward, when it is calm, they will carry you to Euboea, which is a small land far from here, as I have heard from those who once carried Rhadamanthus there in a single day without any effort. Such is the speed of our ships and the skill of our people in sailing. When Ulysses heard such comfort, he was greatly rejoiced in his spirit, lifted up his hands, and prayed thus: "You, highest father Jupiter, grant that Alcinous fulfills all things just as he has now spoken, so that after so many years I may finally come home, and that immortal praise may follow him for it." ### Summary <note>original: "Argumentum"</note> of the eighth book.

A general assembly is held, where it is deliberated and decided 
how the guest Ulysses shall be sent home; the ship is also prepared. Alcinous calls the 
most prominent and best citizens to a feast; in their presence, he bestows much honor 
upon the guest. After the 
meal, they begin to engage in all kinds of pastimes and feats of agility. The skillful poet Demodocus 
sings a song of the love between Mars and Venus <note>The Roman names for the Greek gods Ares and Aphrodite.</note>; then another song of the Trojan 
horse; Ulysses is moved to tears by this. Alcinous takes this as an opportunity to ask the guest 
who he is, where he comes from, and what the cause of his weeping <note>The German "flehens" implies a lament or sorrowful plea.</note> might be.

# The eighth book

He sang of how a disagreement arose between Ulysses <note>The Roman name for Odysseus</note> and Achilles; how they often clashed with harsh, stinging words over the table; and how Agamemnon, a king of nations, secretly rejoiced at their discord.
<margin>The oracle of Pythian Apollo <note>original Latin: "Appollinis Pythij oraculum"</note>.</margin> He sang of how Apollo in Pytho had spoken with Agamemnon and given him a prophecy.

(Homer here calls the city Pytho, which was later named Delphi, situated in Greece and widely famous because of the immense influx and pilgrimage that occurred there from all the surrounding lands to the god Apollo. He had his temple there and a prophetess who gave answers or prophecies to all questions. Agamemnon had also traveled there to inquire about future things, as Homer shows here and as Strabo writes in his ninth book.)

The illustrious poet sang this and similar stories, by which the guests were moved to joy, but Ulysses was moved to sorrow and weeping. For this reason, he pulled the purple garment he was then wearing over his head to cover himself and hide his weeping. But whenever the singer Demodocus paused, Ulysses dried his eyes and let his handsome head be seen again. As soon as Demodocus began to sing once more, Ulysses wept as before under his cloak or mantle. None of those sitting around him recognized the cause of Ulysses’ sadness and weeping except for Alcinous, who, sitting closest to Ulysses, could hear his deep sighing. Laodamas stepped across the grounds to Ulysses, saying: "Dear father and guest, come here among us and let yourself be seen, to show if you have learned such games and contests in your days. <margin>Ulysses's answer</margin>
Ulysses answered: "O Laodamas, I take it as a joke and mockery that you bid me amuse myself with you. In truth, being sorrowful pleases me much better than playing, for I am an unhappy man who has suffered much tribulation until now and has come here in a lowly state, seeking help from you."

<margin>Eurialus's insulting speech.</margin>
Eurialus spoke contemptuously in between: "Guest, I do not take you (by my faith) for any special fencer or fighter, of whom I have seen many in my day; but rather for a sailor or a scout who chases after plunder."

### The Eighth Book

...and finally, she also secretly admitted him into her dwelling and sleeping bed.

Vulcan, a son of Jupiter—as the poets say, and as Homer mentions in the first book of the Trojan War <note>The author refers to the *Iliad*, where Vulcan (Hephaestus) describes his fall.</note>—wished to save his mother Juno from the wrath of his father. Jupiter became enraged, seized him by a leg, and threw him down from heaven so high that he began to fall at sunrise and only touched the earth on the island of Lemnos at nightfall. He dislocated one hip in the fall, and although he remained cast out and despised thereafter, he was nonetheless, by his divine innate nature, more skillful in smithing—the craft he took up—than all other men. He was so wondrous that he was subsequently honored as a god of fire, and the poets praise Vulcan as the master craftsman of all works and weapons that are skillfully wrought through fire and with the hammer.

<margin>Who would dare to call the Sun a liar? <note>original Latin: "Solem quis dicere falsum, audeat"</note></margin>
<margin>The sun sees and brings everything to light.</margin>
<margin>Vulcan’s invisible grates.</margin>
<margin>The island of Lemnos, dedicated to Vulcan.</margin>
<margin>The sleeping together of Venus and Vulcan.</margin>
<margin>Vulcan’s outcry.</margin>
<margin>Vulcan.</margin>
<margin>To see the adultery of one's wife is wretched. <note>original Latin: "Vxoris stuprū videre, miserum"</note></margin>
The Sun reported this affair to Vulcan. Without any further delay, Vulcan went to his forge with a heavy and angry spirit. There, in his rage, he snatched up a heavy, large anvil, set it upon a block, and forged the most subtle, invisible, and unbreakable grates <note>The German "gätter" implies a lattice or grille; in the original Greek, this is described as a fine bronze net.</note> with which he intended to ensnare Mars. When these were finished, he carried them with him and went straight to the bedchamber where the lover's bed stood. He surrounded it all around, above and below, with the aforementioned grates, setting them exactly as one would set a trap for a bird. These grates, as said before, were worked so small and subtly that they escaped the sight not only of men but also of the gods. Once the net was thus prepared, Vulcan pretended as though he wished to travel to his beloved land of Lemnos and departed. Mars, the knight and warrior in his yellow spurs, was keeping a diligent watch; he did not overlook Vulcan's departure and soon found himself with his dearest love. He beckoned to her and led her by the hand, saying: "Come here, my heart's love, let us go quickly to your little bed to rest together; your husband has departed for Lemnos, and we are quite safe from him surprising us." Venus was willing and went with him to their well-known bed of pleasure, and they embraced one another with locked arms and so fell asleep. As soon as they had fallen asleep, the nets—which Vulcan had skillfully fashioned and set over the bed like subtle spider webs—instantly fell shut, and the two were caught in the bed without realizing it. But when they woke up again and could not free their arms—with which they held each other in a hard yet lovely embrace—nor move head or foot, nor pull themselves away or hide, they finally realized they were captured. Vulcan did not travel far but turned back, for the Sun was his spy and brought him the message immediately that the two were ensnared. Therefore, he went to his house in a rage, stood in the forecourt, and gave a fierce, loud cry: "O Father Jupiter and you other immortal gods, come here! See these unjust and shameful deeds; behold how my housewife Venus has forgotten her honor, loyalty, and faith, and has preferred the warrior and lover Mars over her lawful husband because he is healthy and straight-limbed, while I am weak in my thighs and limping. Although I am not to blame for this defect, but rather my parents. Behold, I pray you, how shamelessly they embrace one another and dishonor my marriage bed and bedchamber. O woe is me, poor man, that I must suffer such heartache..."

# The Eighth Book

<margin>Demodocus’s song.</margin> ...began the song, calling upon divine grace, and sang thereafter how several Greeks, throwing fire into their own tents, pretended as if they were departing and wished to travel home again. He sang also how some of them, along with the leader Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>, were shut inside the aforementioned wooden horse and were led onto the highest fortress of the city.

<margin>Three types of judgment over the wooden horse.</margin> Furthermore, he sang how the lords of the city passed three types of judgment over the horse. The first advised: "One should run spears through it." The second: "That it should be cast down from the mountain." This last opinion was followed in the end, leading to the destruction of the city and the entire land of Troy.

<margin>Unchangeable Fate. <note>original Latin: "Fatũ immobile"</note></margin> For it had once been decided in the highest council of the gods that the greatest and most fortified city must be won through a wooden horse. Ulysses, hearing these and similar things sung, became sorrowful in his spirit and drenched his face with many tears; just as a pious, honorable woman bewails her beloved husband, who marches out to protect his fatherland, his little children, and his wife; and as he lies fallen before the city in the sight of his fellow citizens, the pious wife runs out of the city; and when she sees her dear husband writhing on the earth in his own blood and fighting with death, she tears out her hair and cries out piteously; but the enemies pay no heed to this, but instead strike her and lead her away captive. Thus did Ulysses weep heartily, which the others did not notice,

<margin>Alcinous.</margin> except for Alcinous, who sat closest next to him and heard his deep sighing. <margin>The ships of the Phaeacians possess reason.</margin> For we do not place pilots upon our ships, as is the custom among other peoples; rather, our ships have understanding and reason, and understand of themselves the will and the spirit of those they carry, knowing all the circumstances of all lands, cities, peoples, and fields. ## The Ninth Book.

Nevertheless, I will obey you and now give an orderly report on your first, second, and final questions, with a passing account of the heavy and manifold adversities..."

# The Ninth Book

...with which the almighty gods have severely plagued me. And first, hear my name, so that if I should ever escape these dangers and return to my fatherland, you might then know what kind of guest you have hosted. I am Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>, a son of Laertes, famous everywhere for my quick cunning and foresight, and known even unto heaven. My fatherland <image-desc>floral ornament</image-desc> is Ithaca, situated toward the south on high ground near Mount Neritus.

-> <image-desc>manicule pointing right</image-desc> Description of the little land of Ithaca, about which Cicero writes in his *Orations* thus: "And if your fatherland delights you (as is right), which has such great power that the wisest man, Ulysses, preferred Ithaca—situated on a sharp rock like a dove’s nest—even to immortality." <-

<margin>Love of the fatherland. <note>original Latin: "Dulcius est patria nihil atque parentibus usque," meaning "Nothing is sweeter than one's country and parents."</note></margin>
It has many islands around it, namely Dulichium, Samos, and the wooded island of Zacynthus. It is a small, rugged, and hard little land, but excellent for the upbringing of children. I love it more than all the lands I have seen in my days or will see in the future, so much so that neither the malicious Circe could delude or ensnare me with her poisonous magical potion, nor could the most beautiful goddess Calypso persuade me—through enticing gestures, words, and apparent promises—to forget my aforementioned fatherland. The reason is that, by an innate natural quality, nothing is more desirable, sweeter, or dearer to anyone—and especially to one who wanders abroad far from house and home—than one's own fatherland and parents.

<margin>The Ciconians were a people in Thrace, now called Turkey, whose capital city is Constantinople. <note>The author provides a 16th-century geographical context, identifying ancient Thrace with the Ottoman Empire of his own time.</note></margin>

<margin>Battle with the Ciconians.</margin>
For while they indulged too much in the fat mutton and good wine, overloading themselves with food and drink upon the shore, behold, the Ciconians gathered together with their neighboring allies, who were great in number, armed on horse and foot, and strong. They moved against us with their common might in such uncountable numbers, just as flowers and blossoms sprout forth innumerably in the spring. They stormed our ships and forced us into a defense. There, both sides fought manfully, and we held the battlefield (though outnumbered) until well after noon. But as the sun neared its setting, the Ciconians made another attack, by which we were scattered and driven to flight. We hurried to the ships, having lost six men from every ship. # The Ninth Book

<margin>Fertility.</margin> The grain grows in such a way—because their island is so fertile and its soil so rich—that without any manuring, without any toil, cost, or labor, the trees bloom and bear fruit. The ears of grain grow so high and large that at the time of harvest, they bend all the way down to the earth. Their gardens also yield an abundance of wine of their own accord, both summer and winter. Not far from the region just described lies a small, wooded, uncultivated, and deserted island. It is full of wild goats or chamois; no one hunts or catches them because no one can reach them without a ship. Now, the Cyclopes have no ships, nor do they know how to handle them. Furthermore, their own land is so fertile with grain, wine, game, and other necessities, as mentioned above, that they have no need to visit other regions or lands for the sake of nourishment. 

<margin>Description of the port.</margin> This aforementioned island has a most pleasant harbor, overgrown and surrounded by alder trees, in which ships may stand still and safe without being tied down at all. Right next to the harbor, a beautiful cool spring emerges from a high rock. As we came to this port in the middle of the dark night (I believe God willed it so), we saw no island, for the heavens were covered with the thick darkness of the night, and the moon shone quite dimly beneath the clouds. Nonetheless, we landed, wound the sails around the masts, and quickly made our way from the ships onto the land, where we rested and slept until the dawn broke through. <margin>Ulysses’s plan.</margin>
There stood many beautiful, large, shaggy rams covered with black wool. From these, I took the strongest and roughest ones and tied them three and three together (while the giant Polyphemus slept) with willow branches or bast <note>The fibrous inner bark of trees used to make rope.</note>.

<margin>Ulysses hides his companions under the sheep.</margin>
And under every three rams, I bound one man, so that the middle ram carried him and the outer two on the sides helped hold him. Among them all was a ram exceeding all others in length, size, strength, and beauty. This one I grabbed by the back and huddled myself tightly together, hiding myself as best I could under its rough, shaggy belly, yet I never let my bare sword out of my hand. We thus waited under the bellies of the sheep for the dawn with great longing. And as soon as the day dawned, Polyphemus sat—now sick and ill-tempered—in the middle of the gateway. He let only the rams out to pasture, stroking and feeling the back of each one as it went out. The foolish one had no thought or suspicion that we had bound and hidden ourselves under the bellies of the rams. That same ram under which I hid was the very last to go out. Polyphemus felt this one, saying:

<margin>Polyphemus to the ram.</margin>
"O ram, how does it happen that you are the last to go out today, when you are usually the first to the pasture, the first to the water, and the first to be back in the stable? I believe you mourn for the eye of your master, which the quick, cunning 'Nobody' along with his helpers poked out while I slept. But I hope he shall not escape me! And if it is also your intention that I should eat him, then become vocal now and show me where he has crawled off to in fear. Would to God I had smashed his head and brain against a rock; then so much sorrow and pain would not have been inflicted on me by that wicked 'Nobody'!" Speaking thus, he let the ram—under which I lay listening—go out.

<header>The Tenth Book</header>

## Summary of the tenth book.

In this tenth book, Ulysses continues his narrative, showing how Aeolus, a powerful King of the winds, gave him the gentle, fortunate wind Zephyrus <note>The West Wind, known for being favorable for sailors.</note> and bound all the other winds together in a leather bag or sack. However, because his companions opened the aforementioned bag out of curiosity and thus let the winds out, he and his companions were driven backward and came again to Aeolus, from whom they were very poorly received and driven away. Furthermore, they were driven to the giants called Laestrygonians, and subsequently to Aeaea, from where he sent half of his companions with Eurylochus to scout and discover the truth regarding the landscape and its inhabitants. Also, how Ulysses's companions were enchanted by Lady Circe and transformed into swine, but through Ulysses (who received the herb Moly from Mercury <note>The messenger god, known as Hermes in Greek.</note>) they were sought, found, and released again.

---

# The Tenth Book.

<margin>
Description of the Island of Aeolia.

Aeolus, a King of the winds.
</margin>

Afterward, we came to the island of Aeolia, which is fortified and surrounded by a wall and a steep, sheer rock, and for that reason, it cannot be taken by any force. On this island reigns * Aeolus, a son of Hippotes,

> * Aeolus, a King over several islands in Sicily, which are named the Aeolian Islands after him. Because he warned sailors of the ebb and flow of the sea (which in those places is very turbulent and dangerous) and recognized the favorable and contrary winds, he was believed by the ancients to be a king and master of the winds. <note>original: "Vide Strabonem lib. 1." referring to the Greek geographer Strabo.</note>

<margin>Aeolus’s court.</margin>
A friend of the gods, a powerful King of the winds, he has twelve biological children, six of the male and as many of the female sex; these are all joined together in marriage. During the day, the sons live and eat with their lord father, and the daughters with their lady mother, and they live in royal splendor, so that the fire never goes out all day, but rather there is a constant boiling and roasting in the kitchens, a steady coming and going. In the court at night, each brother sleeps by his spouse and sister in silken beds, elegantly covered with beautiful tapestries. When I had entered the city and the splendidly built castle with my companions, King Aeolus received us graciously and kept us honorably and very well at his royal court for an entire month. And he specifically asked me about all things: how Troy was won, with how many ships the Greeks had departed again, and how they came home. I informed the King of his questions one after another as much as was known to me. Then at last, I called upon him, praying that he would graciously grant me his help, so that by means of his kindness, I might reach my fatherland again. Upon this my pleading request, he gave me a bag made from the hide of a nine-year-old ox, in which he enclosed all the stormy winds that were contrary to my journey. <margin>
Destruction of Ulysses's ships and companions.

<margin>
Through Circe, Homer and all poets intend to represent sensual pleasure <term>wollust</term>, which through her sweet drink—that is, physical attractions—makes people beastly, unrestrained, and irrational.
</margin>
There we sailed along the shore and, with God's help, came to a port or harbor where we rested for two days and two nights, for we had become completely exhausted and powerless. And when the morning red <note>the dawn</note> broke forth on the third day, I took my spear and sword and went out to inspect the surroundings. Standing upon a high rock, I saw smoke rising upward from Circe's house in a thick forest or woods. I stood there for a long time in doubt whether I should go there and ask for help; however, it seemed better to me to return first to my ship and companions to receive food. Afterward, I would send out some scouts. Just as I was on my way back, some god took pity on me and drove a large stag toward me, which the heat of the sun had driven out of the forest to seek a spring.

<margin>
Ulysses shoots a stag.
</margin>
I shot through this animal so that it fell, and I quickly placed a braided willow band on its feet. I dragged it through the bushes, over logs and stones, all the way to the ship, for I was not strong enough to lift such a large beast and carry it upon my shoulders. When I had brought it to the shore by dragging it, I presented it to my companions.

<margin>
Ulysses's speech of comfort.
</margin>
And I comforted them thus: "O my dearest ones! Although you are justly troubled, you should not despair, nor wish for death upon yourselves before the appointed hour comes. Instead, endure the adverse storms and the assaults of fortune with patience, courage, and a knightly spirit. And as long as we still have food and drink in the ship, let us satisfy our hunger." Thus I spoke. Thereupon they followed me without delay and sat down one after another on the shore, looking at the wonderfully large stag with amazement. And when they had satisfied their eyes and washed their hands, we prepared a splendid meal, ate and drank happily, and finally slept until it became bright day again. Then I called my companions together and spoke to them with this intent:

<margin>
THE SPEECH <note>original: "ORATIO"</note> of Ulysses.
</margin>
"Dearest and bravest companions, although you have suffered much evil with and by me, and suffer still to this day—so much so that we do not know in what part of the world we are, or where the sun rises or sets—yet do not despair. Let us see where we are sailing under the wide heaven. We will (I hope) soon learn this if you will follow me; for I recently climbed a rock and looked about me. From afar I saw an island, which is surrounded in a circle by the great sea and situated so low that I could see nothing more of it than the smoke."

But to Tiresias specifically, you shall slaughter an entirely jet-black sheep, the very best that I shall give you from my own flock. And when the dead have been thus appeased by you, turn yourself directly toward Hell; slaughter a ram and a black ewe, then walk further along the shore of the river that loses itself in Hell. At once, many souls of the deceased will encounter you. Command your companions to flay the slaughtered sheep, place them on the fire, and offer them first to Pluto and then to his wife, Persephone. You yourself must sit beside the sacrificed meat, holding a naked sword in your hand, and do not let any soul come near the blood until the prophet Tiresias has given you his answer. He will not be long in coming; he will show you the distance and length of your journey, and how you must return home."

And while Circe spoke with me, the morning red of dawn began to show itself. Circe dressed me in a precious garment and cloak; she herself put on a golden robe, covered her head with a silk veil, and adorned herself quite splendidly. I ran quickly throughout the house, waking my companions, calling each one individually by his

name, and encouraging them with gentle words: "Dearest friends, do not let sleep be so dear to you; stand up without delay and be ready to follow the instruction and counsel of Circe." But as friendly as I spoke to them, it was all in vain for one of them.
<margin>Elpenor.</margin>
There was one named Elpenor, a young, unpracticed, un-warlike, and foolish man. Because he was still half-drunk from the previous night's revelry, he stood up in the dark of the morning—perhaps to attend to his needs. And when he heard the commotion of people running back and forth in the house, he was struck with terror; in his senseless, drunken state, he ran backward and fell headlong down a staircase, breaking his neck. When I came upon this accident and saw my companions standing around the

dead body, I spoke to them in this manner: "You perhaps think we are about to sail back home to our fatherland. No; a very different path lies before us, which Circe has shown us. We must first descend into Hell and there make use of the prophecy of Tiresias." At these words, they were seized with such terror and despair that they sat down in sorrow and tore out their hair and beards; but it did them no good.

As Ovid writes, Jupiter and Juno at that time had a "friendly war" regarding the pleasure found in carnal acts. Jupiter claimed that the pleasure and desire of women were greater; Juno, on the contrary, believed that men could less easily do without such pleasure than women. Moreover, God created it so wonderfully that from the lake the most fruitful trees grow, bearing the noblest and most delightful, sweet-smelling fruit—namely pomegranates, bitter oranges, citrons <note>original: "Adams öpffel"; historically referring to various citrus fruits, particularly the citron.</note>, and the like. After that, I further saw the eternal labor of Sisyphus: namely, how he rolls a large millstone up a high mountain with sweat and anguish; and when he has brought the stone nearly to the very top, all his strength fails him, the stone escapes him and runs back down the mountain. Then Sisyphus readies himself again, rolling it back up and laboring at the stone until the sweat runs down over his face and his entire body; and yet this work is ultimately all in vain. Finally, the phantom or ghost of Hercules appeared; for Hercules himself was meanwhile in the company of the other gods in heaven, having the lovely * Hebe sitting at his side.

### Argument of the twelfth book.

Ulysses describes how, after his return from hell, he came again to Lady Circe and was sent off by her in a friendly manner. He sailed past the sweet-singing sea-monsters, the Sirens, and also through the most dangerous places of the Sicilian sea. He landed at the Island of the Sun, wherein his companions—at the instigation of Eurylochus—stole and slaughtered the cattle of the Sun. Because of this, they were all drowned in a shipwreck at sea, except for Ulysses, who swam for nine whole days and nights and only on the tenth day came to the goddess Calypso.

# Homer’s Odyssey
U iii

<margin>The exhortation and warning of Circe. The Sirens are singing monsters <note>original: "monstra"</note> of whom more is said hereafter.</margin>
She gave a gracious answer, and then she spoke further: "Things that have happened are irrecoverable and should be consigned to forgetfulness; henceforth, God will be mindful of you with greater grace, provided you take my teachings and words to heart and follow them. First, flee the sea monsters, the **Sirens**, who are accustomed to softening all men with their singing when they least expect it. They do this so effectively that men forget their wives and small children and no longer think of returning home, for they sing with such exceeding sweetness. They sit upon a green meadow, and beside them lie great heaps of the bones and hides of the dead, which they have stripped from those who listened to them. From this, you may understand what great danger those must ultimately expect who lend their ears to their song. Therefore, before you reach their dwelling, plug the ears of your companions well with wax; and if you yourself wish to hear their song, you may do so. But first, have yourself bound strongly by your hands and feet to the mast <note>original: "segelbaum," literally "sail-tree"</note> so that you cannot break away. Furthermore, command your companions that when you beg them to untie you, they should then pull the bonds much tighter. And when you have sailed past the Sirens and escaped them, I cannot easily tell you which of two paths you should take; the choice must rest upon your own counsel and consideration."

<margin>The rocks called the Cyanean <note>The Symplegades, or "Clashing Rocks."</note> are located not far from Constantinople, situated so close to one another that it is dangerous for ships to pass between them.</margin>
"I must not, however, hide the danger of both paths from you. In one direction are the highest rocks, which are constantly moistened by the seawater. No bird flies over them—not even the doves that carry the herb **Ambrosia**, the food of the gods, to the highest **Jove** <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note>. Much less can any ship pass by without danger, for they are swiftly shattered into ruins in the blink of an eye, and the men and all they have with them are scattered upon the sea by the waves. Only a single ship, called the **Argo**, came through unhurt, and even it would have been smashed had not **Juno** <note>The Roman name for Hera.</note>, the lover of **Jason**, come to its aid. Beyond that, there are two other great mountains or rocks. One reaches up to heaven, so that its peak is hidden among the clouds; no storm, no sun, neither summer nor autumn is ever felt upon it. No man can climb to the peak or height of this rock, nor descend from it, even if he had a hundred hands and as many feet. In the middle of this cliff or mountain, there is a dark cave facing the west <note>original: "nidergang," meaning sunset or the west.</note>, like unto hell itself. O **Ulysses**, stay as far away from this cave as a man might shoot an arrow from a crossbow. For in the middle of that cave dwells **Scylla**, that cruel sea monster, whom no one can look upon without grief and injury; even a god would be terrified of her. She has twelve feet, terrifying to behold; six horribly long necks; and six heads that strike fear into everyone. She has triple rows of broad, thick teeth. She stretches her sixfold heads out of the cave and makes a sound like the howling of dogs; she hunts for porpoises, seals <note>original: "mörhund," literally "sea-dogs."</note>, whales, and whatever else comes before her in the sea. Therefore, no mariner is so senseless as to seek refuge near this cave with his ship, for he knows well that **Scylla** swallows a man with every head and maw. The other cliff or mountain is much lower, and just like..."

## Summary of the thirteenth book.

The Phaeacian citizens transport and bring Ulysses to his homeland, Ithaca; they lay him there while he is sleeping, together with his goods (which have been given to him from all sides), out of the ship and onto the land. Neptune transforms the Phaeacians' ship into a reef; Minerva counsels Ulysses regarding the suitors and gluttons, how they are to be attacked and killed; the aforementioned goddess hides Ulysses's goods in a cleft or cave in the rock, and disguises Ulysses in the form of an old, lowly beggar.

---

who loved me dearly and had given me a house and necessary food—as much as belongs to a servant—and also a dear wife, then my affairs would be well; I would be able to show charity to you and many others. It would be better if Helen and her entire race were eternally perished and wiped out, since for her sake so many brave, noble heroes have lost their bodies and lives." And after such speech, he girded himself with a wide belt, went hastily into the stall in which the young piglets were kept, quickly snatched two of them, sacrificed them, divided them, put them on a roasting spit, and subsequently brought them, thus roasted on the spit, before Ulysses; he sprinkled them with clear flour, poured a sweet wine into the cup, sat down opposite him, and urged him to eat.

# Homer's Odyssey

...well-bred children, I was honored like a god among the **Cretans** and held in high esteem. However, after almighty God called my father from this world, the legitimate children divided the paternal estate among themselves—as the lot decided—and gave me the very least of it. Nevertheless, through my manhood and experience, as well as my practice in the ways of war, I later acquired a respectable wife and a substantial dowry through her. I am now forsaken by these things and, as you can well see, overwhelmed with painful poverty and distress. 

Since **Mars** <note>original: "Mars" — the Roman god of war, representing the Greek god Ares.</note> and **Minerva** <note>original: "Minerua" — the Roman goddess of wisdom and war, representing the Greek goddess Athena.</note> gave me a bold spirit and physical strength, I turned all my practice and diligence toward the ways of war. Whenever I was sent out on an advantage or to a skirmish, many a strong and proud hero fell at my hands; never was anyone found so courageous that I gave him enough breath to attack me first, for I was too quick for them all, overtaking them with my spear. 

Frequent business, labor, and husbandry never pleased me. Only ships, armor, crossbows <note>The original German uses "armbrost" (crossbow), a common early modern anachronism for the ancient Greek bow.</note>, and other deadly weapons gave me pleasure, for I was inclined toward such things by nature. To another man, other arts or practices are dear. Before the start of the **Trojan** war, I held the <term>hauptmanschafft</term> <note>captaincy or supreme command</note> nine times against foreign enemies, by land and sea. Whatever I undertook in the administration of such an office went successfully for me; I gained great honor and captured immense goods, bringing the same home with me from the wars. 

But when the **Greeks**, by the providence and will of the highest ruler and by the common command of the land, marched against **Troy**—before which city many a proud hero remained—I and **Idomeneus** <note>The King of Crete and a commander in the Trojan War.</note> were sent with a number of ships. After we had lain before the mentioned city for nine whole years, and only in the tenth year captured and destroyed it, I sailed home like the others. However, I remained in joy with my wife and children in my domain for no longer than a month. 

Soon after, an expedition to **Egypt** arose. I traveled there of my own will with new ships and many companions. Before my departure, a whole company gathered and joined me. When we had spent six days in joy, eating, drinking, and offering sacrifices, we set sail from the land on the seventh day with a favorable wind. On the fifth day after our departure, we arrived in Egypt without any mishap and landed our ships on the shore of the river. 

There, I sent out some of my companions to scout. But they, being overwhelmed by their own strength and power, acted differently and more aggressively than they had been commanded; they fell upon the country folk, plundered the fertile fields of **Egypt**, carried off women and children as captives, and miserably killed the men who put up a defense. When the cry of this reached the nearest city, young and old rose up. At the first light of day, they marched against us with such irresistible power that all the surrounding fields were filled with soldiers on horse and foot. My companions were seized with an excessive terror and immediately took flight. Some were slain in the flight, but many...

### Summary of the fifteenth book.

Minerva appears to Telemachus in a dream, urging him that he should return
home without delay. Telemachus obeys, takes his leave of Menelaus, and 
receives great gifts. And when he had sat down in the ship, there comes by chance Theoclyme-
nus, a seer; he takes him as a companion; they come thus together to Ithaca.
Near the city, Telemachus disembarks from the ship and goes into the house of Eumaeus,
his father's swineherd; the others sail on the ship to the city of Ithaca.

### The Fifteenth Book ###

...give gifts that you can easily and well carry with you on the wagon. I will also command that you be given a breakfast <note>original: *frůmal*; the text emphasizes that one should not travel a long distance on an empty stomach</note>, for it is not good to travel far while fasting. And if you wish to take your path directly through Greece, I will personally escort you with horse and wagon, leading you through beautiful cities to princes and great lords, none of whom will let you depart without honor or a gift.

<margin>Telemachus’s answer.</margin>
Telemachus spoke: "Menelaus, I am firmly resolved to stay away from home no longer. For while I search in vain for my father and find him nowhere, I fear that I might either lose my own life in a foreign land or lose my property at home." When Menelaus understood this intent, he ordered his wife <note>Helen of Troy</note> to command the servants to prepare the breakfast. Etheoneus, a son of Boethis, had also just risen; Menelaus told him to build a fire, set the meat, and roast it. Then he went with Helen and his son Megapenthes into his treasury. There, Menelaus took a silver bowl and gave his aforementioned son Megapenthes a silver beaker to carry. Helen drew forth a small chest in which lay many veils that she had woven herself. From among these, she sought out one that lay at the very bottom, which was the most beautiful and most precious of all; it was made of pure gold and glittered like a star.

<margin>Menelaus’s gift.</margin>
They returned with these gifts to Telemachus, and Menelaus began to speak thus: "Telemachus, may Almighty God grant you a fortunate return. I shall give you from my treasure a silver bowl, which the god Vulcan <note>original: *Vulcanus*; the Roman name for Hephaestus, the god of fire and smithing</note> skillfully crafted, and which the King of the Sidonians <note>original: *Sidoniorum*; refers to the people of Sidon in Phoenicia</note> gave to me when I was once his guest. I ask that you keep it for my sake." With these words, he placed the bowl into Telemachus's hand. Megapenthes likewise set the beaker down before him. Helen stood holding the golden veil in her hand, saying: "O son, take here the work of my hands. This shall be a pleasing gift for your future wife; remember me by it when you return joyfully to your beloved fatherland." Telemachus received the gifts one after another and handed them to Pisistratus <note>the son of Nestor, traveling with Telemachus</note>, who looked upon them with great wonder and locked them in a traveling chest <note>original: *beleiẞ*; a sturdy bag or chest for transport</note>. After this handover, Menelaus led Telemachus and Pisistratus back into the royal hall and seated them on precious chairs. A servant poured water over their hands from a golden pitcher into a silver basin. The gentle, chaste housekeeper <note>original: *schließerin*; literally a 'key-bearer' or female steward</note> laid bread and meat in abundance upon the prepared table and blessed the food for those eating. Etheoneus carved the meat and served it; Megapenthes poured the wine. And when they had eaten and drunk to their satisfaction, they rose again from the dining couches. Telemachus and Pisistratus harnessed the horses and drove out of the royal house, coming to a halt before the courtyard. There Menelaus came after them, carrying a large bowl of wine in his right hand. Standing before the wagon, he said: "You young lords, be blessed; and tell Nestor that he is unforgotten by me, for he was like a faithful father to me when we Greeks lay before Troy." To this, Telemachus replied:

"What you command us, we will tell them, and we shall faithfully carry it out. And if God helps me return to my land, I will not keep silent about the great kindness, honor, and goodness shown to me in your court, nor how richly you have gifted me." And as they spoke thus, an eagle came flying from the right hand side, carrying in its claws a large white hen, which it had taken from the nearest poultry-house or nest. Women and men ran after the eagle, intending to hunt the hen away from it, but the eagle flew toward the wagon and landed nearby. All who saw this were filled with joy. Pisistratus <note>The son of Nestor, traveling with Telemachus</note> spoke: "Most excellent Menelaus, consider and observe whether this vision announces future things for us or for you." Menelaus reflected on how he might interpret this well and correctly, but Helen interrupted and spoke:

<margin>Helen’s Interpretation.</margin>
"Listen, for I will tell you what God inspires in me and how I understand it: as a prophecy. Just as the wild eagle has torn the domestic bird or goose, so too shall Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>, who has wandered long and suffered much, finally come home. He shall severely punish the suitors who fill and fatten themselves in his house; indeed, he has already decided within himself how he will destroy them." Telemachus prayed to the highest gods, Jupiter and Juno <note>original: *Jouem vnd Junonem*; the text uses Latin names for the Greek gods Zeus and Hera</note>, his wife, that Helen's prophecy might come true. After these words, he threatened the horses with the whip; they ran through the city and then across the heath all day long, unharnessed. When the sun went down and it became dark, they saw the city of Pheras <note>Pherae</note> and turned in to

<margin>Pheras.</margin>
the house of Orsilachus, staying there overnight. And when they were gifted by Orsilachus in the early morning with presents (with which guests are customary honored) and it had become day, they harnessed the horses once more and drove them forward with the whip. The horses, running swiftly, brought them in sight of the city of Pylos <note>original: *Pilum*</note>. Halting there before the city, Telemachus addressed Pisistratus thus: "Pisistratus, a son of Nestor, we have been bound together first by the love and friendship that extends from both our fathers, and subsequently by our own acquaintance as two of the same age; and now this journey has made us even closer. Therefore, I ask you as my good friend, companion, and fellow traveler: please leave me here by the ship and do not lead me with you into the city, so that your father does not delay me for long, for I must return home in haste." These were his words. Upon this, Pisistratus considered how he might grant his request; he drove the horses to the shore and carried the gifts—the clothing and gold with which Menelaus had gifted Telemachus—into the ship. He then turned toward him, saying: "Board quickly and sail away before I reach my father’s house. I know the old man’s mind and spirit well; he would certainly not let you depart without gifts. Indeed, as old and experienced as he is, he would even come out here himself with his weak legs to lead you back inside. I also know well that he will be quite angry and annoyed with me for letting you go." After saying

this, he drove toward the city and arrived at his father's house. Telemachus urged his companions thus: "Dear companions, bring out all the ship’s tackle and prepare yourselves for the journey; let us board without delay and complete our way."

# The Fifteenth Book

<margin>
The memory of past evils is a delight. <note>original Latin: "Præteritorum malorum recordatio delectat." This refers to the idea that once a hardship is over, it becomes pleasant to recount.</note>
</margin>
...let everyone rise for their work; we two will remain, and each will lament his sorrow to the other. For he who has wandered far and suffered much in his days finds a certain joy in speaking of his endured and past misfortunes. Therefore, I shall begin to tell you what you desire to know from me. 

<margin>
Syros.
</margin>
There is an island called Syros <note>original: "Siria," referring to the Greek island of Syros in the Cyclades</note> (perhaps you have heard of it), not very large, but so fertile in livestock and grain that neither want nor hunger appears there. Also, the air is so temperate that no person dies of any illness there; rather, when the inhabitants of the said island grow old, Apollo and Diana <note>The Roman names used by the translator for the Greek deities Apollo and Artemis</note> go about with their bows and shoot those who have lived their time <note>A poetic way of describing a peaceful, natural death in old age</note>. The island has two cities, where all things are held in common and shared among the people; both of these were subject to my father, Ctesius, son of Ormenus <note>original: "Ctesio Ormenidi"</note>. My father's wife, my mother, was a native of Phoenicia <note>an ancient civilization in the Levant, famous for maritime trade</note>, a beautiful, stately woman who knew how to perform exquisite handiwork. 

<margin>
Phoenicians.
</margin>
Now it happened at one time that her countrymen, the Phoenicians—a shrewd and deceitful people <note>original: "überflüssigs volck"</note>—came there with ships, bringing many strange wares which pleased the women, leading their minds astray and beguiling them. And when my mother had gone out to the water to see the strange merchandise, and was washing her feet in a secret place by the water, one of the men came upon her, had his way and pleasure with her, and afterward asked from where and how she had come into this land. She answered immediately and said: "I am from Sidon <note>original: "Sidan," a major Phoenician city-state</note>, a daughter of the wealthy Arybas <note>original: "Aribanti"</note>; long ago I was captured in the fields by Taphian robbers, brought here, and sold to an old man with whom I now dwell." He spoke to her: "I know your parents well, and I know how rich they are. Come now, dear one, prepare yourself and sail back with us to your parents." The woman was willing and said, "Yes, indeed; if you promise me that you will bring me home, I will go with you." They promised her this on their faith and honor, and then she spoke thus: "We must proceed very quietly and discreetly with the matter, so that I (should my husband find out) do not fall into eternal imprisonment and you all into ruin. Therefore, keep our plan secret among yourselves; buy your necessities in the city, and if I happen to meet you on the street or at a well, do not speak to me; act as if you do not know me. And when you have finished your shopping and have loaded the ship with food and drink, let me know by a messenger. Meanwhile, I will gather together silver, gold, and whatever I can; I also have a very handsome, clever, and nimble little boy, born to a good father, whom I will bring with me, for he likes to run about and has a desire to travel to foreign lands." 

After these words, my mother went home again. When everyone stood and was silent, Antinous, the son of Eupithes, began such a speech:
<margin>Speech of Antinous.</margin>
"Dear friends, God and no one else has protected Telemachus. We lay on high watch day and night, one alternating with the other, making our observations to see how we might catch and kill him. However, as previously stated, he has escaped us all and come away with his life. But we should not yet cease, but rather use every cunning so that he does not escape our hands. For as long as he lives, we shall achieve nothing here; he will also cause us great and destructive enmity among the <term>common people</term> <note>original: "poffel"; the general public or populace of Ithaca, derived from 'populace'.</note> through his complaints. a silence, except for Amphinomus, the son of King Nisus, who was the most notable among all those present from Dulichium. Let us first seek the counsel of the gods, and if they themselves decree the death of Telemachus, then he shall die by my own hands and weapons. But if the gods do not consent, then I will be neither guilty nor partaking in the murder that you have in mind." The opinion of Amphinomus pleased the majority well, and they stood by it. They then parted from one another, went back to the royal court, and sat before the gate on the marble benches. After this, the evening meal was held; they ate and went to sleep.

# Argument <note>original: "Argumentum"; a summary or synopsis of the plot to follow.</note> of the seventeenth Book.

Telemachus returns home and recounts his travels <note>original: "peregrination"</note> to his mother Penelope—where and with whom he had been, and what he had discovered. ### The Seventeenth Book

No one knows how these matters will yet end. For if the Suitors should perhaps strike me down at home (as is their plan) and divide my property among themselves, I would much rather the gifts remain in your power than that they should also fall to them as their share. But if I (as my hope in God <note>The translator uses "Gott" (God) in the singular, reflecting a 16th-century Christianized interpretation of the divine power</note> stands) prevail and they are slain, you shall bring the aforementioned gifts to me yourself in joy when the time is right. After these words, he led the foreign guest away, and when they had come home, they took off their clothes and prepared for the bath. And when they were cleansed, the bath-maids poured sweet-smelling water over their bodies, and they dressed in fresh laundry. Coming thus from the bath, they sat at the prepared table. A servant held a golden hand-basin and gave them the water for their hands over a silver bowl. The diligent housekeeper brought forth the food in full supply; they ate. Penelope sat opposite on an ornate chair, by the door, spinning a very fine thread upon a distaff. And when everyone was satisfied, the aforementioned chaste woman began to speak thus.

<margin>Penelope.</margin>
Telemachus, it is weary for me to go to my bed so early, which, since the departure of your father Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>, my dearest husband, has never been dry of the tears from my eyes. Therefore I pray you, tell me, since the Suitors are not here now, what you have heard anywhere of your father’s return. Telemachus answered:

<margin>Telemachus tells his mother of his voyage.</margin>
Mother, I will inform you rightly. We first traveled to Pylos, where King Nestor received us honorably in his high castle, and treated us kindly, like a father whose dear son returns home from foreign lands after a long time. But regarding Ulysses my father, whether he be alive or dead, he could give us no certain report; therefore he sent us further to the honorable Menelaus, where I saw Helen, for whose sake alone so many Trojans and Greeks <note>original: "Kriechen"</note>, by divine will and destiny, have miserably slain one another. When Menelaus asked of my journey and arrival, and I hid nothing of the truth from him, he finally cried out thus: "It is an everlasting shame that godless and bellicose people presume to sleep in the marriage-bed of the most powerful man, Ulysses. Truly, just as a wild deer or hind carries her suckling first-born fawns into the lair of a great-hearted lion, and as soon as the lion returns from the forest, he tears apart the mother, the young and the old; so shall it go for the Suitors with Ulysses. O highest father Jupiter <note>original: "Juppiter"; the Roman name for Zeus</note>, I wish Ulysses were present now in the same form as I saw him at Lesbos wrestling with Philomelides, whom he overcame and threw hard to the great jubilation of the Greeks. He would undoubtedly make the wedding bitter for the Suitors and give them all a quick end." <margin>Theoclymenus prophesies to Penelope about Ulysses.</margin>
In response, Theoclymenus spoke: "O most noble lady, Telemachus does not have a full and complete understanding of this matter. Therefore, hear me; I will prophesy to you without any fabrication, by the highest God <note>original: "Gott" — the translator uses the singular "God" here, reflecting a 16th-century Christian lens on the Greek Zeus</note>, and by this table and house which I have entered as a guest: it is the certain truth, as I prophesied from the wondrous vision that appeared to Telemachus on the ship, that Ulysses is in his fatherland on this very day and hour, either wandering or resting. He understands the shameful and wanton deeds of the Suitors <note>German: "Werber," those seeking Penelope's hand</note> and is even now contemplating and striving for their destruction."

<margin>Penelope to Theoclymenus:</margin>
Penelope spoke: "O guest, if your prophecy were to come true through its fulfillment and in deed, you would surely recognize my gentle gratitude toward you and be so richly gifted by me that everyone would call you wealthy and blessed." Thus they spoke with one another. Meanwhile, the Suitors were amusing themselves in front of Ulysses's court; some shot with steel bows <note>original: "ståheln" — likely referring to the steel of crossbows or steel-tipped arrows, a 16th-century anachronism for the ancient Greek bow</note> or arrows, while others threw stones on the wide, pleasant courtyard, which they had previously often dishonored and defiled through their wanton and insolent behavior.

<margin>Medon’s speech to the Suitors.</margin>
When it was now time for the evening meal, and the livestock came in from the pastures from all sides along with the shepherds, Medon—the most prominent among the stewards <note>Medon was the herald of the palace</note>—ran toward them, calling out: "You young noblemen, you have now refreshed your spirits with games and pastimes; now come to the evening meal. It is not pleasant to play during the time for eating; it is good to eat on time." They all rose, went into the house, took off their cloaks, slaughtered the fat goats, pigs, and sheep, and prepared the meal.

<margin>Ulysses and Eumeus prepare for the journey.</margin>
Ulysses prepared himself for the road. Eumeus spoke to him, saying: "Guest, your mind is still set on going into the city today. I would have gladly kept you here as a fellow-servant, but since my master <note>Telemachus</note> has commanded me to lead you there, I must do so, in order that I may avoid his anger. For masters become harshly angered, and often for slight cause. Therefore, it is time for us to be on our way; the greater part of the day has passed; in the evening the cold sets in, and the road becomes worse the longer it takes."

<margin>Ulysses to Eumeus.</margin>
Ulysses answered: "I know and understand myself that it is as you say. Therefore, you shall perceive no delay from me; only lead me, and I will follow you bravely. But give me a staff somewhere that I may lean upon. For, as I have just noted from you, the path is slippery and slick." Speaking thus, Ulysses hung an old, dirty sack around his neck and girded himself with a notched, crooked sword. Eumeus handed him a walking staff, and they set out on their way; the other servants and dogs guarded the sheepfolds. Eumeus led his master, in the unrecognized form of a pitiful, ragged beggar. They came to a pleasant fountain near the city, which is much visited by the inhabitants to draw water.

And first, a fountain was established by Ithacus, Neritus, and Politor. All around it stood many alders and poplars, which were kept moist by the flowing spring water. # The Seventeenth Book

Pliny, in the eighth book, chapter 40, states: Of all animals, the dog and the horse are the most faithful to man. After many accounts of such loyalty, the aforementioned author concludes that only dogs recognize their master, even if he returns home disfigured, neglected, and unrecognizable <note>This refers to Ulysses's return in the guise of a beggar, where only his old dog, Argus, truly knows him</note>. Only dogs (I say) perceive the voices of the household, understand their names, and remember the paths they have once run. After man, no animal has a sharper memory. Similarly, Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a Roman writer on agriculture</note> says: What servant loves his master more than a dog? Where is there a more faithful traveling companion, where a more vigilant watchman, or a guardian who is less likely to be overcome by bribes and gifts? Finally, where can a servant be found who so diligently protects and avenges his master?

<margin>Eurymachus’s mockery</margin>
Eurymachus wished to make himself seem witty, and began to speak of <term>Ulysses</term> <note>original: "Vlyssem"; the Latinized name for the Greek hero Odysseus</note>, saying: "Take note, you noble <term>Suitors</term> <note>original: "Werber," refers to the men competing for Penelope's hand</note>, the gods have sent this guest into the house of Ulysses so that he might light up the darkness with his bright, bald head." And after such insults, he turned to Ulysses and said, "You seem sturdy enough of heart to earn your keep; if you wish to be my servant, I will hire you. You must, however, perform all the labor on my fields—repair the broken fences and plant trees. In return, I will let you have no lack of bread, clothing, and <term>meat</term> <note>original: "sawfleisch," literally sow-flesh or pork</note>. But I fear you are too corrupted for work, since you have become accustomed to idleness and begging."

<margin>Ulysses’ response.</margin>
To this Ulysses answered: "If, in the autumn during the long days, we were to work fasting side by side until the dark of night—each of us mowing the <term>late hay</term> <note>original: "grůmet," the second harvest of hay in a season</note> with a curved scythe, or if we were to plow four fields in a morning with four strong oxen—you would soon see which of us could make the better or straighter furrow. Also, if God were to send a war upon this land, and I had a shield, two good spears, and an iron helmet, I would stand at the very front of the line. But you merely despise me now, calling me an insatiable glutton, thinking to win glory thereby and showing yourself a mighty hero through your contempt for my person—yet you only keep company with ill-mannered people. Truly, if the master of this court, Ulysses, were to come home, all the gates—wide and broad as they are—would become too narrow for you to flee through."

<margin>Eurymachus to Ulysses.</margin>
Eurymachus took these words with resentment, gave Ulysses an angry look, and said: "I believe, beggar, that you are full of wine, for you utter such bold words among so many men without any fear. If I knew it were your nature to always speak así, you would suffer misfortune at my hands this very day." And with these words, he snatched up a stool and threw it at Ulysses. He missed him, but hit the cupbearer on the right hand, so that he spilled the cup of wine onto the ground. The cupbearer fell to the earth, whimpering and carrying on most piteously. The Suitors ran about the hall, putting their heads together and saying: "What devil brought this vagabond in here, who causes one disturbance after another and destroys all our joy?"

<margin>Telemachus’s speech.</margin>
Telemachus stood up for the beggar and spoke: "You restless men, what misfortune makes you so unruly that you rise up from eating and drinking? Whether you are drunk or merely full, go home; yet I do not wish to drive anyone away." They were startled by the speech of Telemachus, and bit their lips and teeth together in anger.

<margin>Amphinomus.</margin>
Amphinomus then spoke: "Friends, henceforth no one should show this guest any further annoyance or shame. Nor should anyone attempt to trouble or drive out either this man or any other in Ulysses’ house. Come, butler, bring out the wine; let us drink a final toast and offer a sacrifice so that we may go to sleep. Telemachus will surely know how to look after his guest." They all agreed with one voice. The herald Mulius, the servant of Amphinomus, poured the wine and passed the cups around.

## Summary of the nineteenth book.

Ulysses and Telemachus carry all the weapons and gear into the <term>armory</term> <note>original: "harnaschkamer," literally a chamber for harnesses or armor</note> and arrange them ready at hand. Penelope comes forth from her bedchamber and asks the guest about his lineage and fatherland. He feigns that he is from the island of Crete, born of the lineage of King Minos. He is recognized by <term>Eurycleia</term> <note>original: "Euricleam"; Odysseus's old nurse</note> as she washes his feet, by the <term>scar</term> <note>original: "masen," a mark or physical sign</note> on his leg, but it is not made public. Furthermore, the poet relates how and where <term>Ulysses</term> <note>the Roman name for the Greek hero Odysseus</note> received the scar on Mount Parnassus. Penelope reveals her dream to the guest and desires him to interpret it for her.

<margin>Crete is now called Candia; it came under the rule of the Venetians in the year 1194.</margin>
* **Strabo** and generally all geographers give the island of **Crete** a hundred cities, except for **Homer**. But in our times, no more than ten cities are counted in **Crete**, among which is the capital city **Candia**, from which the whole island takes its name.

Consecrated or dedicated to the highest god **Jupiter** <note>original: "Joui"</note>, it is situated in a very beautiful and pleasant location, fruitful and populous; for within it are found ninety well-built cities, all inhabited and settled by peoples of different languages—namely by the **Achaeans**, **Eteocretans**, **Dorians**, **Cydonians**, and the widely-famed **Pelasgians**. And of all these aforementioned peoples and cities, **Knossos** <note>original: "Gnosus"</note> is the most highly renowned, not only for its exceeding size, but also because King **Minos** held his reign there for nine years.

<margin>**Knossos**, formerly the foremost city on the island of **Crete**, built by King **Minos**, had a circumference of thirty stadia <note>An ancient unit of distance; the text equates it to a "horse-run."</note>. Strabo, book 10.</margin>
**Minos**, a king of the island of **Crete**, gave his subjects wholesome laws; and so that he might create belief and authority for them, he went for nine consecutive years into a cave, claiming that he held conversation there with the highest **Jupiter** and had written the laws from his inspiration. Read **Aelian** in his *Various History* <note>original: "Aelianum de varia historia," a collection of anecdotes by the 2nd-century Roman author Claudius Aelianus.</note>.

Your Ulysses wore at that time a double-layered purple cloak, adorned with a golden brooch and golden buttons throughout. It featured an exquisite embroidery of gold and silk, depicting a hunting dog holding a young fawn <term>rechpöckel: a small deer or kid</term> in its teeth, so skillfully sewn that they seemed to live—the fawn appeared to want to escape the dog with its front legs. However, I do not know for certain whether Ulysses brought said tunic from home with him or if he received it somewhere on his journey or from the spoils of war. For he had many friends and few detractors; indeed, I myself—if I may say so without boasting—gave him a sword, a purple tunic, and a new ship. To give you even more signs: a well-aged herald followed him everywhere. He had curly hair, a dark complexion, and broad, rounded shoulders.

# The Nineteenth Book

Lady, wife of Ulysses, I have no desire for soft bedding, having been completely unaccustomed to it since the time I sailed from Crete. I can well lie upon a hard bench (as I have done until now) and pass the entire night without sleep until the bright morning. Furthermore, I have no desire to bathe, nor shall any young maid touch my feet, unless it be an aged, sensible woman who has suffered as much as I; before such a one I would not hesitate to bare my tired legs.

<margin>Penelope.</margin>

# Summary of the twentieth book.

Ulysses prays to the gods for two miraculous signs, by which he might be strengthened to punish the wicked suitors. Ctesippus throws an ox foot at Ulysses during the meal, but does not achieve his intended purpose. Theoclymenus, because of his prophecy by which the final destruction of the suitors was indicated, was driven away with scornful mockery.

---

## The twentieth book.

Ulysses prepared a place to lie for himself in the forecourt from the raw hides of the sacrificed oxen and sheep, and lay himself upon them; Eurynome threw a garment over him, under which he, while resting, thought of this and that, making many plans as to how and when he should attack the suitors. The unchaste housemaids <note>original: "haußdiernen," referring to the disloyal female servants</note> acted lewdly in the court, running back and forth, joking and laughing. At last, one after another stole away from the house, each to her secret lover. Ulysses noticed this in time and thought for a long time whether he should creep after them on their path, or allow them to fulfill their evil desire together for the last time. 
<margin>Simile.</margin>
And just like a female dog that has recently given birth, while she has her young under her, snarls at every stranger with a desire to attack them; so he growled and burned within himself, entirely greedy for revenge and punishment against the unfaithful and vice-filled suitors; he beat his breast out of great displeasure, rebuking himself and saying: "Ulysses, have patience and remember that you previously suffered much more
<margin>Ulysses speaks with himself. This was spoken of above in the ninth book.</margin>
and overcame it with patience, namely on the day when the inhuman, one-eyed giant Polyphemus swallowed your brave companions before your eyes; from which cave you alone, through your quick-wittedness, escaped along with several of your companions and were rescued from deadly peril." Thus spoke Ulysses to himself, tossing the thoughts back and forth in his heated mind, no differently than a man turns a roast on a spit by the fire. Minerva came from heaven in the form of a woman, stood by Ulysses, and spoke: "You most troubled man,

why do you afflict yourself with excessive fantasies and waking without ceasing? ### Summary of the twentieth book.
<note>original: "Argumentum"</note>

Ulysses prays to the gods for two miraculous signs, by which he might be strengthened to punish the wicked suitors <term>Werber<note>The noblemen competing for Penelope’s hand.</note></term>. Ctesippus throws an ox-foot at Ulysses during the meal, but he does not achieve the purpose of his intent. Theoclymenus, because of the prophecy by which the final destruction of the suitors was indicated, is driven away with mocking insults.

## The twentieth book.

Ulysses prepared a place to lie for himself in the forecourt, made of the raw hides of the sacrificed oxen and sheep. He lay down upon them, and Eurynome threw a garment over him, under which he rested while thinking of many schemes, back and forth, as to how and when he should attack the suitors. The unchaste housemaids were frolicking in the courtyard, running here and there, jesting and laughing. At last, one after another stole out of the house, each to her lover. Ulysses noticed this in time and thought for a long while whether he should sneak after them on their way, or permit them to fulfill their evil lust with one another for the last time.

<margin>A Simile.</margin>
And just like a female dog that has recently given birth, while she has her young ones under her, snarls at every stranger with a desire to attack them; even so he grumbled and burned within himself, entirely greedy for revenge and punishment against the unfaithful and vice-ridden suitors. He beat his breast out of great indignation, rebuking himself and saying:

<margin>Ulysses speaks with himself. This was mentioned above in the ninth book.</margin>
> Ulysses, have patience and remember that you have previously suffered more and overcome it with patience; namely, on the day when the inhuman, one-eyed giant Polyphemus <note>The Cyclops who imprisoned Ulysses and his men.</note> swallowed your brave companions before your very eyes, from whose cave you escaped only through your quick-wittedness, along with several of your comrades, and were rescued from deadly peril.

Thus Ulysses spoke with himself, tossing the thoughts in his heated mind back and forth, no differently than a man turns a roast on a spit by the fire.

<margin>The Speech of Minerva.</margin>
<note>original: "ORATIO Minerue"</note>
Minerva came down from heaven in the form of a woman, stood by Ulysses, and spoke: "You most weary of men, why do you afflict yourself with excessive fantasies and waking without ceasing? You are now in your own property; you see your faithful spouse and your only son, your blood and flesh, before your eyes, which should rightly bring you delight."

<margin>Ulysses' answer.</margin>
Ulysses answered: "O Goddess, you speak rightly; but nonetheless I must be anxious, cautious, and well-deliberated as to how I shall tackle this difficult matter with advantage, firstly so that I, being alone, may prevail over so many of them. Also, secondly, if God grants me the victory (as I hope), where and to

To this, Minerva <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Athena, who often appears to Ulysses in disguise or as a voice of wisdom.</note> replied: "O Ulysses, you have often trusted a weak, helpless, mortal man; how much more rightly should you place your trust in me, as a heavenly, immortal goddess of wisdom, who has never forsaken you in any concern but has been helpful and supportive in all your needs. Therefore, let your vain mourning be, and give your exhausted body its necessary rest; for to remain awake through the entire night is no small suffering." After these words, she clouded the eyes of Ulysses with a gentle sleep and returned again to heaven. Now that I am awake, the joy I had in my sleep is extinguished."

---

Among the soothsayers, it has been held and believed that thunder and lightning occurring so usefully and in a clear, bright sky signify good fortune for the actions undertaken at that time. Ulysses was not terrified by this, but rather much more gladdened.
