I wish that for the gluttonous suitors <note>original: "Werbern." The men pressuring Penelope to marry one of them while consuming Ulysses' estate.</note> he would signify that today is their last day on earth and the last time in Ulysses' house, so that I, a poor, powerless little woman, might also finally come to rest; for I have been so worn down for a long time now with grinding, baking, cooking, working, and waking, that I must pay for it with death." Ulysses heard these words clearly, rejoiced in his spirit, and thought of the revenge against the suitors. Meanwhile, the house servants stood up, as did the beautiful and gracious youth Telemachus; he also rose from his bed, dressed himself, girded on a sharp sword, took a long spear upon his shoulder, stepped forward, and called to Eurycleia, saying: <margin>Telemachus's command.</margin> "Dearest little mother, see that you do not forget the guest; provide for him with food, drink, and all necessary respect as is fitting. You must not rely on my mother in this; though she is otherwise a very knowledgeable woman, yet out of great distress she holds this lack of judgment: that she sometimes offers discipline and honor to a rogue, and meanwhile lets the worthy man depart empty-handed and unrewarded." Eurycleia excused her mistress, saying: "Dearest son, you should not attribute any guilt to your mother. She left the guest no lack of food or drink; moreover, she commanded the housemaids to make him a soft bed. But he would not accept such a thing; instead, he remained overnight under the sky in the forecourt, lying upon the raw hides of the slaughtered cattle." ## Summary of the twenty-first Book.

Penelope promises herself as a future wedded wife to the one who can span <note>To "span" or string the bow, a feat requiring immense strength.</note> the bow. Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> reveals himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius; he commands them to guard the doors so that they let no one either out or in. When all the Suitors <term>Werber</term> <note>The men competing for Penelope's hand.</note> fail at the bow, Ulysses finally strings it without any special effort; he shoots through the hatchets or axes, and thus reaches the goal.

# The twenty-first book.

The goddess Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena, often used in 16th-century translations.</note> put it into Penelope’s mind that she should present the bow and arrows of Ulysses to the Suitors, thereby giving them a cause and a beginning for the battle. Therefore, she took the key and went up the stairs; she opened the treasury, in which much worked and unworked gold, silver, and many kinds of bronze lay locked away.
<margin>The bow of Ulysses</margin>
In that room, the curved bow was also kept, which Iphitus—along with a heavy quiver filled with many sharp arrows—had given to Ulysses as a gift (when they met by chance at Messena in the house of Ortilochus).
<margin>Messena.</margin>
For after those of Messena had taken and stolen about three hundred sheep, together with the shepherd, from the citizens of Ithaca some years before, they were required by a treaty to give the Ithacans a yearly tribute. Ulysses was sent there while still quite young to collect it; and it happened that at that same time, Iphitus also traveled to Messena to seek his twelve lost mares

<margin>Hercules, a murderer of his guest Iphitus.</margin>
...to seek [the horses], which then miserably cost him his life and limb; for when he had recovered the aforementioned mares and stayed overnight with the great-hearted hero Hercules, the said son of Jove <note>original: "Jouis"; the Roman name for Zeus</note> grew so excessively fond of the mares that he set aside the fear of the gods, trust, and faith, and committed a murderous evil against his friend and guest. Ulysses did not take the aforementioned bow with him to war, but left it at home as a very worthy and pleasant gift and a memory of his dear friend. Penelope (as has been heard) released the key from the ivory ring or clasp on which it hung, inserted it into the lock, gave it a push, and immediately the large, well-secured iron door swung open with such a loud sound, like an ox bellowing in the open field; then she went further into a chamber where, on one side, many clothing chests stood, and on the other, armor and weapons hung.

<margin>Penelope brings forth the bow of Ulysses.</margin>
She took the bow from the peg, unwrapped it from the case with which it was covered, sat down, laid the said bow on her lap, and began to weep bitterly, asking the bow where its master was. And when she had shed many tears over the bow and made her vain lament, she then took her way to the Suitors <term>Werber</term>, carrying the often-mentioned bow in one hand and the quiver in the other; her court maidens did not go empty-handed either, each carrying a bag with iron rods <note>These are the iron axe-heads through which the suitors must shoot.</note>. And when they came to the hall or banquet house of the Suitors, she stood at the threshold and spoke thus to them.

<margin>Penelope’s speech.</margin>
"You noble, proud youths, hear and understand me well: you have been lying here for a long time now, eating and drinking, and consuming another's property, justifying your unjust dealings with me. Now I will no longer let this accusation rest upon me, but will finally be rid of you, and have therefore now agreed to take one from among you—whoever is powerful enough to span <note>To "span" or string the bow, a feat of great strength.</note> this bow of my dear husband; you may try yourselves at this." She commanded the swineherd to place the bow and the arrows in the middle of the hall. When Eumaeus and likewise the ox-herd saw their master's weapon, tears fell freely from their eyes; Antinous rebuked them thus:

<margin>Antinous to the herdsmen.</margin>
"You coarse fools and field-trolls! Stop your weeping; it is unnecessary to move Penelope to memory of her former husband, whom she otherwise thinks of more than enough and will not forget at all. Therefore, sit down or get out; weep then until you are weary of it, but leave the bow to us, to prove our mastery upon it. I can well imagine that many a man will grow tired and fail at this, for (to confess the truth) a man like Ulysses (as I saw him once in my childhood) will not easily be found among us, nor anywhere else far and wide." Thus he spoke with his mouth, yet in his mind he presumed he could span the bow; he thought of nothing less than that he would be the first to taste the bow—he who, with mocking and instigating, had always been the first against Ulysses. # Book XXI

...since she has offered herself to all of you, both together and individually, as the prize of this contest, it is unnecessary to mirror or praise the virtues, lot, honor, and renown of my mother with ornate words. For you know yourselves, and must confess, that her equal among women is found neither in Pylos, Argos, or Mycenae, nor in the whole land of Achaia and Ithaca. Therefore, be undaunted; reach diligently for the contest, so that it may be openly recognized how earnest and eager you are for my mother. I will also not delay, and will try my hand at my father's weapon <note>original: "wōr"; likely a variant of "Wehr" meaning weapon or defense</note> to see if I might win my mother away from you and keep her here myself. And saying this, he cast off his purple mantle, drew his sword, and with it made a long trench or furrow straight as a line; into this, he set the axes <note>The "beihel" are the twelve double-headed axes through which the suitors must shoot an arrow.</note> and banked them with earth so that they stood upright toward the goal. The Suitors <term>Werber</term> were struck with wonder at Telemachus’s great skill. He then reached for the hand-bow and attempted to string it three times, and three times he let it go again. At the fourth attempt, he would have undoubtedly strung it with great force had Ulysses <note>original: "Vlysses"</note> not signaled to him; because of this, he once again willingly desisted, turning toward the Suitors with these words: "I find well that I, as a young man, am too weak and not sufficient to win my mother from you; I leave this place to you as the stronger ones." He then laid the bow upon the table and sat back down in his chair.

<margin>Antinous speaks.</margin>
In response, Antinous, a son of Eupithes <note>original: "Epethei"</note>, stood up and spoke: "Companions, just as we are accustomed to sit and draw lots at the table, let us also stand and shoot in order, one after another." This proposal pleased them all collectively.

<margin>Leiodes a soothsayer.</margin>
The soothsayer Leiodes, a son of Oenops <note>original: "Oenepi"</note> (who always made a habit of distancing himself from the others because he took no pleasure in their dealings), was the first to stand up. He took only the bow but immediately placed it back in its spot, saying:

<margin>Prophecy of Leiodes.</margin>
"I will grant it to another, for whoever tries his hands on this bow will truly—unless all my art deceives me—find that it will become the heartbreak of many, costing them body and life." After such words, he sat down again in the chair from which he had risen.

<margin>Antinous rebukes Leiodes.</margin>
Antinous rebuked him with harsh words, saying: "Leiodes, you have spoken a womanly and immoderate speech in saying that none of us shall string this bow, as if we must all perish over it. Because you were born so weak of your mother and are so unskilled in stringing and shooting, you should have thought that many others are here who are more capable, to whom that which you cannot achieve gives no trouble at all."

<margin>Antinous to Melanthius.</margin>
After these words, he turned toward the goatherd Melanthius and spoke: "O Melanthius, quickly make us a fire; set a stool or seat beside it, lay a cushion upon it, and then bring a large lump of lard <note>original: "schmår"; tallow or animal fat used to soften the wood and string of the bow</note> so that the young heroes may grease and warm their limbs, and thus be able to string the bow with greater strength." When the Suitors had now eaten, lived well, and anointed their limbs, they were nonetheless just as unable to master the bow as before. Antinous and Eurymachus, being the most powerful and the leaders of the entire crowd, held themselves back from the bow for a time, lest they perhaps fall into shame and mockery...

Because of this, amidst the wedding joys and the wine, a murderous shedding of blood occurred between two famous peoples—namely, the Lapiths and the Centaurs—so that many of both sides remained dead. The main culprit, Eurytion, was struck dead with a beaker <note>original: "pecher"</note>; this 'dry blow' <note>A "dry strike" often refers to a blow from a blunt object or an unexpected, bloodless hit that proves fatal</note> is described quite excellently and effectively by Ovid in the twelfth book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>original: "transformationum"</note>.

Thus, acting like any other raging and senseless man, he committed so much misconduct that the other lords and guests could not endure it; they dragged him by his feet out of the house and cut off his ears <note>original: "ozen"</note> and nose. From this, a great bloodshed subsequently arose between the Centaurs and the Lapiths. Just as Eurytion, through his excess of wine, led himself and others into destruction, so it shall happen to you as well. ### The Twenty-First Book

<meta>catchword: Argument</meta>

Following the command of Telemachus, the housekeeper Eurycleia was told to lock the door so that no one might go out or in, which she diligently did. Philetius also went out secretly, took a large board and leaned it against the door, and further bound the lock and the bolts with a heap of rope. Ulysses turned the bow here and there, inspecting it everywhere with diligence to see if it were still whole and if any part had been gnawed by mice or rotted away in such a long time. The Suitors mocked him, one saying to another: "Look, dear companions, how our wretched beggar admires the bow; how precisely he inspects it! I believe he is a bow-maker, or intends to become one, and is studying the bow to learn." Another said, "If he could not beg and mooch 
<margin>Ulysses strings the bow.</margin>
better than he can string a bow, he would soon die of hunger." Their mockery gave Ulysses no concern; rather, like a skillful harper when he takes his well-known harp in hand, pulls each string, and tunes it high or low to his pleasure, so Ulysses tested the string of the handbow, strung it, and released it again without any effort. ## Summary <note>original: "Argumentum" — a traditional scholarly term for a plot summary at the start of a chapter.</note> of the twenty-second Book.

Ulysses, in the presence and with the divine help of Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena, the goddess of wisdom and war, who champions Odysseus.</note>, slays the Suitors and finally punishes the disloyal and unchaste household servants.

### The twenty-second book.

After Ulysses stood up and cast off his tattered rags, taking the bow and quiver into his hands, he stepped forward into the midst of the Suitors. First, he poured the arrows out onto the ground beside his feet, and standing thus with the drawn bow among the Suitors, he spoke. <margin>Ulysses’s speech to the Suitors.</margin> "Until now, every one of you has been safe from my shooting; but now I will test myself and see if, with the help of Apollo <note>Apollo was the patron god of archery; the contest takes place on his feast day.</note>, I can hit the mark and the true target which no one until now has reached." And with these words, he let the deadly bolt <note>original: "strahel" — literally "ray" or "beam," used here poetically for an arrow.</note> fly at Antinous <note>original: "Antinoum" — the first and most arrogant of the suitors.</note>, who at that moment had no fear of a sudden death. It struck him straight through the throat, so that the cup he had just raised to drink from fell from his hands; the table and the food were overturned, and the hall was drenched in blood. 

Because of this unforeseen act, an exceeding terror seized the Suitors; they swarmed together, running back and forth, looking here and there at the walls for weapons. But when they could see or find neither shield nor any means of defense, they addressed Ulysses with such insulting words: <margin>against Ulysses</margin> "O stranger,

# The XXII Book

"How hit-home <note>original: "heimisch" — literally "homely," here meaning a blow that strikes close to home or is unexpectedly familiar.</note> and wickedly you attack us with your arrows! Who would have expected such treacherous feats of combat from you? The most noble and well-born youth in all the land has been robbed of his life by your hands and bolt; but truly, this shall be the last time you do such a thing, for your own unavoidable end now stands before your eyes. You have nothing more certain than that you must leave your body here as food for the ravens and other greedy birds." Thus they grumbled with words against Ulysses, yet they did not lay a hand on him, for they all still thought the shot had missed its mark against his will. They did not know that the hour of their destruction had come and the punisher was at hand.

<margin>Ulysses answers the Suitors.</margin>
Ulysses looked at them defiantly and with anger, saying: "You dogs! How is it that you had so little concern that I would ever return to this land? Therefore, without any shame or fear of God or men, you presumed to squander my goods so lavishly, to lure my virtuous wife to your ways, to violate my maidservants, and thus shamefully dishonor my house and court. For this you must now all pay the penalty here, and all die by my hands." They all turned pale <note>original: "ergilbten" — literally "turned yellow," describing the sallow look of sudden terror.</note> at this speech and were struck dumb, so that they could not speak a word. They sought a way to flee, but Eurymachus alone took heart and spoke.

<margin>Eurymachus lays all blame upon Antinous.</margin>
"If you are indeed a Prince of this land, then you have the right and justice of the matter; for the shameful conduct of the Suitors with which they have burdened you is plain to see. But Antinous was guilty of all this, he who incited us to it and who sought the young life of your only son, hoping not only to inherit your chaste wife but also your land and lordship—which the highest God did not permit him. Therefore he has received his reward and lies there dead in a piteous state. Since this is so, and the cause of the committed evil has been punished, spare the rest of your people. Have mercy on us and spare our bodies and lives; in return, we shall show ourselves eternally grateful to you. We are willing to repay twenty-fold for all the harm we have caused you through eating and drinking or in any other way, until you are fully satisfied." To this, Ulysses gave an angry and terrifying—

<margin>Ulysses’s answer.</margin>
—countenance, along with these words: "Eurymachus, all the wealth that you now possess or might possess in the future would not be enough to move me to spare you. You must either defend yourselves against me by force, or escape through flight, or else die by my hands. Choose from these which you prefer." At this speech, their courage turned cold, and their knees and whole bodies trembled like aspen leaves.

<margin>Eurymachus to his companions.</margin>
Eurymachus spoke to his companions thus: "There is no hope that this man, since he has once begun, will stop shooting at us until he has killed us all. Therefore my advice is: prepare yourselves for defense, unsheathe your swords, throw the tables up as shields against his murderous arrows, and rush at him in a crowd to see if we can drive him from the door and raise a cry and tumult in the streets, whereby he might be stopped." And with these words, Eurymachus drew his sharp two-handed sword <note>original: "baidenhädter" — a Renaissance-era weapon, reflecting the translator's own time rather than Homeric Greece.</note> and pressed toward Ulysses with a murderous cry.

<margin>Ulysses to Telemachus.</margin>
Telemachus did not delay; he brought four shields and as many helmets adorned with dyed horsetails and plumes, as well as eight spears; with these he first armed himself, then the servants for war; they stood thus in their armor beside the stern and resolute hero Ulysses, who shot among the Suitors as long as he had arrows, so that they fell in heaps one after the other; and when the quiver was completely emptied, he leaned the hand-bow against a wall, hung about his shoulders the bucklers or shields that were covered with four ox-hides, placed upon his head the terrifying iron helmet, and took a spear in each hand.

# The Twenty-Second Book

...[who] carries weapons to the suitors; who, even now, so far as I am able, shall die by my hands, or be captured and delivered bound to you, so that he may receive the well-deserved punishment for the many and long-practiced wickednesses he has committed in your house. Ulysses said: "We will hold the ground here against the suitors and let none of them escape. They obeyed the command of Ulysses, bolted the door of the armory <note>original: "harnaschkammer" — a room where armor and weapons were stored.</note> wherein Melanthius was searching for weapons. And as he tried to come out, carrying a beautiful helmet in one hand and an old, neglected targe <term>targe: a small, round shield used for defense</term> in the other—which Laertes had been accustomed to use when he was still young—they shoved him so that he fell backward over the threshold. They grabbed him by the hair and threw him with all their might onto the ground, binding his hands and feet; they hoisted him by a rope high up to a beam and left him suspended there, just as Ulysses had commanded. Eumeus mocked him with these and similar words: "Melanthius, on this soft bed <note>Eumeus is being sarcastic; the 'soft bed' is the uncomfortable rope and beam where the traitor is hanging.</note> you shall keep the night watch, and you shall by no means sleep through the dawn, so that you may drive the goats and cattle early to the suitors to be devoured, as is your custom." After this, Eumeus and the other servants went to Ulysses, standing around him, breathing hard with stiffened resolve. <margin>The Suitors' speech</margin>

But if you make yourself a part of this war and show them help, you shall be as dear to us as they are; we will not be satisfied until you are dead, and we shall forcefully seize all your property and goods in the city and in the country, and divide them among ourselves, and moreover banish your wise son and daughters from the land." 

<margin>Minerva.</margin>
Minerva grew angry and spoke to Ulysses in a rebuking tone: "Ulysses, where is your manliness and knightly spirit that I recognized in you nine years ago, when we fought for the beautiful Helen at Troy? Then, many brave men fell by your victorious hand, and the great, powerful city was conquered solely through your military counsel and cunning schemes. Now the time and final necessity demand that you show your strength, power, and high wisdom—with which you are more richly gifted by the gods than others, and which you have often shared with strangers in the past—for the sake of yourself, your wife, and your son, to save your rule and your possessions. Therefore, be undaunted; stand here at my side, and see what a hero Mentor, son of Alcinoi, is."

With this speech, Minerva promised victory to neither side (as the outcome was still doubtful) but instead only encouraged the spirits of Ulysses and his companions. She then transformed herself back into the shape of a swallow and flew onto a high roof, sitting opposite Ulysses. On the opposing side stood Agelaus, Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisandrus, and Polybus, who, acting as the leaders, exhorted the other knights to fight gallantly for their bodies and lives and to win honor. And principally, Agelaus made such a speech to them:

<margin>The speech of Agelaus. <note>original: "Agelai oratio"</note></margin>
"O you worthy companions, Ulysses' boldness has now diminished! Mentor <note>The goddess Minerva had been disguised as Ulysses' old friend Mentor earlier in the scene.</note> has merely puffed him up with idle words and has departed. They will not stand for a moment. Therefore, since we have no lack of projectiles, let six arrows be shot at them in nimble haste to see if one might wound Ulysses and earn the reward. The others will give us no trouble once Ulysses alone is dispatched." As soon as Agelaus concluded his exhortation, they diligently loosed six strong projectiles at Ulysses. But Minerva struck the arrows aside, so that one stuck in the upper threshold, another in the door, and the third in the wall. Seeing this, Ulysses spoke: "Dear friends, now it is our turn; shoot into them, into those who seek to deprive us of our bodies, honor, goods, and lives." Telemachus shot through Euriades, the swineherd <note>Eumaeus</note> through Elatus, and the oxherd <note>Philoetius</note> through Pisandrus. The suitors hurriedly plucked the arrows from the dead bodies and shot again at Ulysses and his supporters.

<margin>Telemachus is wounded.</margin>
But Minerva turned them away as before, so that they all missed their mark, except that Amphimedon’s arrow touched the palm of Telemachus, grazing the skin slightly; Ctesippus also hit the swineherd upon the shield, so that he fell to the ground. After this, the suitors took flight, hiding themselves in the corners. Ulysses did not let up from them; he stabbed Eurymedon and Amphimedon, while Polybus was mortally wounded by the swineherd.

<margin>The death of Ctesippus. All is repaid.</margin>
The swineherd split Ctesippus' chest open and spoke mockingly to him: "That is your reward for the ox-foot with which you pelted Ulysses in the hall, when he was asking you for alms in the guise of a beggar." Then Ulysses ran through Demestorides with a long spear. Telemachus split the spine of Liochritus <note>Liochrito</note> so that he fell down upon his face. Then Minerva appeared, hovering on high with her terrifying shield <term>shield: the Aegis, a divine emblem or shield that, when shaken by a god, paralyzed enemies with terror</term>, at which the suitors were frightened beyond measure. Just as oxen in the long, hot days—when the gadflies <note>original: "premen"</note> sting—run about raging among one another, so the suitors scattered in flight. They even struck their heads against the walls, sighing and crying out piteously. And as the great Egyptian hawks hunt the small birds in the valleys and fields, seizing and tearing them with their sharp claws, so did Ulysses pursue the fleeing suitors into every corner and chamber; and whoever came under his hands was killed, so that dead bodies lay in all corners and places, and the whole house was drenched with blood.

# The Twenty-Second Book

...and receive me, falling at your feet, into your grace. By my honor and faith, I have never pursued any woman at your court with words or deeds, but always advised against it—though they did not follow me and have therefore been justly wiped out. But I, a seer, come to an innocent end if I must lie dead among them. O God, how there is no gratitude or repayment on earth for kindnesses rendered!

<margin>Ulysses' answer to Liodes. <note>Liodes (or Leiodes) was the sacrificial priest and seer for the suitors.</note></margin>
Ulysses looked at him angrily and spoke: "Since you boast of being their seer, you should have known for certain that I would return to this land, and you should not have presumed to woo my wife. Therefore, you shall not escape bitter death." He took up the sword that Agelaus had thrown away and struck off Liodes' neck in the middle, so that the head jumped away while it was still speaking.

<margin>Phemius begs for mercy.</margin>
<margin>The office of a poet.</margin>
The skillful singer Phemius—whom the suitors had forced to stay with them and entertain—stood with his harp by the door, doubting whether he should flee into the courtyard to the Altar of Jove <note>Original: "Jouis" (Jupiter/Zeus). The altar in the courtyard was a sacred place of sanctuary where a person could not be legally harmed.</note> (where there was freedom and safety) or fall at Ulysses' feet. As he thought back and forth, God put it into his mind that he should lay down his harp and stretch himself out at Ulysses' feet, saying: "Ulysses, hear me and let me find grace with you. I am a poet and singer, perfected without any master and learned through divine inspiration <note>Phemius claims to be "self-taught," a sign in the ancient world of being directly inspired by the Muses or gods.</note>, to praise the glory of the immortals and mortals. Therefore, I am held in high regard and dignity among men like another god, and it would undoubtedly cause you regret before long if you were to stain your hands with my innocent blood. For your son Telemachus can well inform you that I did not join your court out of presumption, nor for the sake of begging or food, but because the suitors overwhelmed and forced me to serve and sing before their table."

<margin>Telemachus saves Phemius's life.</margin>
Telemachus heard Phemius’s pleading words and spoke quickly to his father: "Restrain yourself from laying hands on this innocent man, and also on the herald Medon, who always loved me and took great care and notice of me while I was still small. I only fear he is gone, that Philetius or Eumaeus has already executed him, or perhaps you yourself, Father, if he came under your hands in your fury."

<margin>Medon is also interceded for.</margin>
Medon, who out of fear had crawled and hidden himself under a leather chair, heard these words quickly; he crawled out, embraced Telemachus's feet, and spoke: "Friend, here I am; pray your father that he does not act hastily against me."

<margin>No good deed goes unrewarded and no evil unpunished.</margin>
Ulysses smiled and pointed to Telemachus, saying: "For the sake of his intercession, I will grant you your life, so that you and others may say how much better and more profitable it is to do right than wrong. And so that those who do right may enjoy it in their time, while the wicked and unjust must pay for their malice. Therefore, go, you and the poet together into the forecourt; wait there until I have finished all things in the house." They went to the altar of Jove and sat there in safety and sanctuary in great anxiety, looking around often, as those who still fear death. among whom are twelve unchaste women who cared for neither me nor Penelope. Telemachus was young, and his mother did not want to trouble him with complaints about the maids. # The Twenty-Third Book

The courtyard rang and echoed. From these words, Ulysses understood that she intended to test him; he answered as if in anger: "Wife, I would be very dissatisfied if I were placed in any bed other than my own, which I made <margin>Ulysses describes his sleeping bed.</margin> with my own hands. I decorated it with gold, silver, ivory, and fine furs, and placed it in a new chamber built of stone. The bed is fixed upon the olive tree and fastened with nails in such a way that no one is strong enough to move it, even with the greatest effort. This should be a sufficiently credible token for you."

Thus, had he remained with her, she would have wished to make him not only rich and happy, but also immortal in body and unfailing in youth; finally, he concluded with the account of how he sailed away from Calypso, and after many dangers swam naked and bare to the shore of the Phaeacians, was admitted before King Alcinous, and was regarded as a god, gifted with much gold, silver, and clothing, and sent back to his land upon a ship.

### Summary of the twenty-fourth book.

Mercury leads the souls of the slain suitors into the underworld. Agamemnon / Achilles / and Amphimedon enter into conversation / and one tells the others of his pitiful end and the cause of such death. Laertes finally recognizes his son Ulysses. An uprising occurs against Ulysses led by the kinsmen of the slain. But the same is settled without great bloodshed by Minerva.

---

# The XXIV Book

After Ulysses <note>original: "Vlysses," the Latin name for the Greek hero Odysseus.</note> had been absent for many years and everyone had despaired of his return, we (as you see us present here) courted his wife. We waited in constant hope, but she neither promised nor rejected anyone; instead, she gave everyone modest words, through which she led us to the ruin of body, property, and life. In addition to 
<margin>Penelope’s Trick.</margin>
all this, she also devised a practical trick: she began a large, subtle weaving or fabric and spoke thus to us: "You young lords, since my husband Ulysses (God have mercy) is deceased, it is my prayer that you grant me this respite and delay regarding the wedding, until I have first completed the work I have begun, so that the warp threads do not remain or perish in vain upon the loom. This is so that my injured father-in-law Laertes, when he is eventually called from this world, may then have an honorable shroud <note>original: "leichttũch," a winding sheet or burial cloth.</note>, so that I may not be judged poorly or as unseemly by the Greek women. For it would be wrong if I let the old man—who in his lifetime labored much and earned much wealth—be laid to rest in the earth without a special shroud appropriate to his rank, like any other common craftsman or citizen." With these and similar subtle words, we allowed ourselves to be led astray. But however much she wove throughout the long day, she unraveled it again by candlelight at night. She carried this on secretly for three whole years, until it was finally revealed to us in the fourth year by a housemaid; we then caught her at it and forced her to finish the work. As soon as she had completed the aforementioned shroud—which was truly beautiful, fine, and like the brightness of the clear sun—the matter reached the point where Penelope, having no further excuse or delay, was to choose one of us as her lawful husband. Take note: then truly our evil angel led Ulysses here from foreign lands. He first stopped for shelter with his swineherd <note>original: "sawhirt," referring to the faithful Eumaeus.</note>, where his son Telemachus also unexpectedly arrived, having sailed from Pylos. They made themselves known to each other and deliberated how they might seek their advantage and kill us. Telemachus went ahead into the city; the swineherd led Ulysses after him, dressed in torn, beggarly clothing, in an old, sick, and so inconspicuous form that none of us—not even the elders of the people—recognized him. Because of this, we forgot ourselves and treated him with mocking words and even blows, all of which he bore with patience until Jupiter <note>original: "Juppiter," the Roman name for the Greek king of gods, Zeus.</note> ignited his spirit with a desire for revenge. There, he arranged with his son Telemachus to lock away all the weapons and also plotted with Lady Penelope to bring out the great hand-bow of Ulysses and the sharp arrows; she did this, thereby providing the beginning of the battle. For when we each especially tried our hand at it, not one of us was strong enough to string it. But when Ulysses had brought the bow to his hands, he strung it without any effort, poured the arrows out before him on the ground, and looking terribly around him, let the projectiles fly swiftly at us. He first shot King Antinous, and then one after the other, so that one fell here and another there, in his blood

When Amphimedon had thus finished speaking, Agamemnon cried out: "O blessed Ulysses, noble
<margin>Agamemnon.</margin>
son of Laertes! Thanks and praise shall be spoken to you, for you have—as befits a strong and steadfast hero—so earnestly avenged your chaste wife, who remained faithful to you. Through this, she has earned eternal glory among gods and men, so that the fame and report of her chastity, marital loyalty, and womanly virtue shall never be forgotten by those who come after, and she shall be praised and sung as a crown and ornament of the female sex. But Clytemnestra, a daughter of Tyndareus <note>original: "Tindari," the earthly father of Clytemnestra and Helen of Troy.</note>, has left behind a shameful reputation, and words hateful to all honorable, honor-loving women."

While the souls in the underworld <note>original: "hell." In this era, the Greek Hades was often translated as "Hell," though it refers to the general realm of the dead rather than a place of punishment.</note> were thus speaking with one another, Ulysses arose and went out of the city to the pleasant field which his father Laertes himself had built and cultivated. Upon it stood a house, fenced and enclosed on all sides, in which Laertes had his dwelling with his old cook-maid and the servants whom he used daily for labor. 

<margin>Ulysses goes to his father.</margin>
When they came near to the house, Ulysses spoke to his son and servants: "Go into the well-built dwelling; slaughter for us the best sow that you find in the stable. I will betake myself into the garden to my old father and try whether he still knows me." With that, he gave his word to the servants, and they went into the aforementioned house. 

When Ulysses came into the pleasant field, he found neither the steward Dolius, nor his sons, nor any servants at home, for they had all gone out to gather stones. He saw only his old father Laertes, crawling about in the vineyard, pruning the vines, dressed in a worn-out garment, covered with a hat made of goatskins <note>original: "geißfellen."</note>, wearing boots and rough gloves. 

Although he was misshapen and wasted away from age and sorrow, Ulysses nonetheless recognized him at once. He stood still for a while under a large tree, weeping profusely, and doubted for a long time whether he should fall upon his father's neck, make himself known to him, and recount what had befallen him and how he had fared before he came back to his fatherland. He finally decided within himself that he would approach his father with questions. 

<margin>Ulysses to his father.</margin>
He went straight to him and said: "O old man, I perceive you have a special understanding of how to build, plant, and tend gardens; and just as the work praises the master, so your diligence and great skill show themselves. These fruitful fig, olive, and pear trees, as well as the grapevines and other plants, truly do not grow without the special toil and care of the gardener. But you must forgive me: while you are devoted to the garden, you forget yourself, afflicting your lived-out age with labor, care, and sorrow, which you might well be spared. For in your form or physiognomy <note>original: "phisonomey," an archaic term for one's facial features and what they reveal about character.</note> you do not look like a servant or day-laborer, but much more like a King, if only you were dressed in royal garments, washed, and adorned. But if you are indeed a servant, then I pray you, tell me: to which master are you bound in service, to whom..."
